chapters.title: The First Breath
paragraphs: The child moved before Elara was ready to look at him.
Something small scraped against her dress. She felt it through the damp cloth, a tug near her knee, and tried to lift herself on one elbow. Pain tightened low in her belly. Her arm gave way.
For a while she could only lie there and breathe.

The opening in the rock had become a patch of white. Snow blew across it, thinning whenever the wind changed, then thickening until she could no longer see the ground outside. She listened for the baby. There should have been a cry, something she would know how to answer.
Instead came a soft, uneven snuffling.

She reached for the strip of linen she had brought to wrap him in. One end had fallen into a crack in the rock. She pulled it free and shook it with a clumsy snap, as if a clean cloth were still the thing that would put everything in order. She had hemmed it by the window. There was a crooked corner where she had worked after the light failed, too impatient to wait until morning.
She spread that corner over her palm. The snuffling came again, nearer this time.
She lowered her eyes.
At first she saw the colour: pale pink against the grey of her skirt. Then a narrow head lifted, and the folds along its back opened a little. Light showed through them. They were wings.
Elara stopped breathing.
The creature pulled one foot free of the cloth. Its claws caught in a seam. It tugged, slipped, and tried again, making the same thin noise. Each attempt brought it a little closer to her.
She drew her leg away.
The movement hurt. She gasped, and the little head jerked towards the sound.
“No.”
Her voice was so faint she barely heard it herself.

She looked past him at the rock, then at the white opening. She had come into this place carrying a child. She could remember the weight of him beneath her ribs. Even now her body seemed to remember it, though the weight was gone.
Perhaps she had fainted. Perhaps there was something she had not seen.
She searched the folds of her dress with a shaking hand. The movement brought her fingers close to his face. He turned towards them at once.
Elara snatched them back.

His wings trembled. They seemed too large for him, thin and awkward, the edges still folded over themselves. One lay against her skirt; the other dragged along the stone. She could see the effort of his breathing beneath the tiny scales at his throat.
He was looking at her.

She had imagined looking back. Not this face, not these eyes, but the moment itself: someone small and helpless meeting her gaze, waiting for her to do whatever mothers were supposed to know how to do.
She pressed her hand over her mouth.
The creature made a sound again. He had freed his claw and managed another uncertain step. His head bumped her knee. He remained there, leaning against her, as though the journey had exhausted him.
Elara could not make herself touch him.
She could not stop watching his chest, either. When his breath caught, hers caught with it. She waited until the next one came.

There was a place on his breast where the scales were so fine she could see the skin move underneath. She fixed her eyes on it. Up, down. When she looked at the wings she wanted to crawl away; when she looked at that little patch, she wanted him to take another breath. She could not make those wants agree.
Beyond the opening, the wind lifted loose snow from the ground. She turned towards that brightness, measuring the distance without meaning to. A few steps. She would have to stand first.
Her palm found the rock behind her.
The little head followed the movement.

There was no one else in the cave. She looked again, because the thought that someone might be there, someone who could tell her what had happened, was harder to surrender than she expected. Only the rock, her scattered clothing and the child.
Her child. The words recoiled from what lay against her leg.

She pulled her shawl towards her. One corner had been trapped beneath her hip. Freeing it took an effort that left her sweating in the cold. She worked without looking down, folding the cloth across her shoulders, tucking one end beneath the other. A familiar task. Her hands knew how to do it.
The snuffling stopped.

In the sudden quiet she heard something else, a faint scrape. The little creature was trying to climb over the fold she had pulled away from him. One foreleg reached up; the other could not find purchase. He tipped onto his side.
Her hand moved before she decided to move it.
It stopped an inch above him.

He righted himself. A wing folded underneath his body, and for several breaths he struggled to pull it out. She watched, her hand suspended, until he had done it. Then she drew her fingers into the shawl.
“I don't know what you are,” she whispered.
He answered with the same small sound.

She had heard stories. Everyone had. The kind told near a fire when the door was barred and whatever lived beyond it belonged safely to the dark. In those stories a person always knew what a creature wanted. Hunger, treasure, the destruction of a village. There was a name for it and a way to kill it.
Nothing had prepared her for one that could not manage the hem of a dress.

Elara braced a foot against the stone. She pushed herself upright in stages, stopping when the cave swung around her. The shawl slipped; she caught it. When she could see clearly again, the small head was raised towards her face.
He had not moved away.

That frightened her more than if he had hissed or struck. There was an expectation in his attention. Whatever she had brought into the world had brought a need with it, and she was the only living thing it knew.
She slid her skirt from beneath him.
He followed the cloth until his feet met bare rock. The movement set his wings fluttering. She stepped back, and the sound he made changed.
It was not loud. It did not have to be.
“Stop.”

She did not know whether she was speaking to him or to the feeling rising inside her. She turned towards the entrance and put a hand to the wall. Stone bit into her palm. She welcomed it. She could understand the sharpness of stone.
Outside, the cold took her breath so thoroughly that for a moment she heard nothing at all.
The slope fell away towards the valley. Her footprints were still visible in the snow, though their edges had softened. She put her foot into one and steadied herself. Then the next.
Behind her, from inside the rock, came the thin, persistent cry.
Elara tightened the shawl across her chest and took another step.

chapters.title: Back Through the Snow
paragraphs: She kept her eyes on her feet.

The snow ahead of her had a grey crust. Where she broke through it, darker water gathered around the edge of her boot. There was a way down between the stones. She had come up it. She needed only to put one foot where the other had already been.
The cry grew fainter.
She waited for relief. It did not come. Her body was still listening. Each time the wind dropped, she heard him again, and her shoulders tightened as though someone had called her name.

Below lay the village. Roofs, smoke, doors she could knock on. If she reached them, someone would make her sit. Someone would bring water and ask what had happened. She could say the child had died. Babies died. People understood that terrible ordinary thing.
They would be kind to her.
The thought carried her a few more steps.
Then the cry stopped.
Elara stood still.
Wind moved across the slope. A little snow slipped from an overhanging stone. She could hear her own breathing, rough and too fast. There was no sound from the cave.
She told herself that he had fallen asleep.

She knew nothing about him. Perhaps he slept when he was cold. Perhaps rock was where such things belonged. There might be another creature somewhere in the mountain, one that would know how to feed him, one whose body was the same as his.
But she had been alone in the cave.
Her fingers tightened on the wool. She could still feel the bump of his head against her knee. Not an attack. He had crossed the stone because she was there, and when he reached her he had rested.
She turned halfway, stopped, and looked down the slope once more.

The village smoke had thinned into the low cloud. From this distance she could not distinguish one house from another. She thought of the questions. Where was he? Had she wrapped him? Had she closed his eyes?
She would have to answer without knowing whether he was still breathing.
Elara went back.

Halfway through the turn, she caught herself rehearsing an explanation for the empty arms with which she would enter the village. The words had been easier to find than a way to hold him. That was what stopped her making another bargain with herself. She put the nearest roof behind her and faced the rock.

She did not run. Her body would not let her. The return was a slow, stumbling climb in which every stone seemed higher than it had on the way down. Once she went to her knees. She stayed there until the pain eased, then pushed herself up with both hands.
At the cave mouth she stopped again.
He lay where she had left him, his neck stretched towards the light. Snow had blown a little way over the threshold. There were grains of it on the tip of one wing.
She dropped beside him.
His eye opened.

The breath went out of her in a sound almost like anger. She had been angry all the way back: with the mountain, with her own weakness, with him for being impossible. Now she was close enough to see the tiny movement at his throat, and there was nowhere for the anger to go.
“Oh,” she said.
He lifted his head. It wavered, too heavy for the narrow neck, then settled against the stone.
Elara took off the shawl.

The cold reached her at once. She spread the wool across her knees and slid one hand beneath his chest. This time she did not withdraw it. His skin was not like a fish's, as she had feared. The little scales were smooth in one direction and faintly rough in the other. Between them, at the join of neck and shoulder, she could feel warmth.
He moved, and she nearly dropped him.
“Wait. Please.”

His forefoot caught her sleeve. She loosened each little claw from the weave, afraid of breaking something, afraid of being bitten, afraid of everything she had no name for. At last she had him against the wool with one hand beneath his body and the other supporting his narrow breast.
He fitted into her arms.

That was the fact she could no longer avoid. Not comfortably, not in the way she had imagined, but he fitted. The weight found a place against her. His head tucked into the space below her collarbone, and the little claws loosened.
Elara bent over him.
She began to cry so hard that she could not see the entrance.
He pushed his nose against the wet skin beneath her chin. She laughed once, a broken sound that hurt her throat. The tears did not stop. She held him more securely and let them fall into the cloth.
“I came back,” she told him.
It was not a defence. He did not know she needed one.

When she could stand, she folded the shawl around them both. She left room for his face, then covered it when the wind struck, then uncovered it again to check that he could breathe. Her hands kept moving. Too tight, too loose, a wing caught in the fold. She had to learn each thing separately.
The way down took longer with him in her arms.

At the first steep turn she had to sit. There was no safe way to use both hands on the rock while he lay against her breast. She lowered herself onto a ledge, tucked her skirt beneath her and eased down the last stretch on her heels. He wriggled when the shawl tightened. She loosened it, felt a gust reach his face, and tucked it back around his body with a smaller opening at the top.
“That will have to do.”

He settled against her heartbeat. She stayed where she was for a moment, looking at the short distance she had managed. The village was still far below. Bringing him back had not made her suddenly strong or taught her how to carry him. It meant she would have to work out the next few feet, and then the next.

She kept to the rougher edge of the path where stone gave her boots something to grip. When he stirred, she stopped. When he made a sound, she looked around, though there was no one on the slope. At a bend above the first houses, she drew the cloth higher.
The creature inside it objected.
“Only a little while.”

She could not carry him openly through the village. That knowledge had arrived without argument. She could barely look at him without fear; she could not ask everyone else to understand him at a glance.
Elara took the quieter way between the houses.

Familiar things looked altered by what she carried. A window was a place someone might appear. An open gate forced her to turn her shoulder. The scrape of a shovel stopped her until she knew which yard it came from.
At her own door she had to choose which hand to free.

He wriggled beneath the shawl while she fumbled with the latch. She pressed him closer, murmured something without words, and at last got the door open with her shoulder. The room beyond was dim and cold.
She shut them inside.
For several breaths she leaned against the wood, holding him. No voices followed. No knock came. The room smelt of old smoke and the wool she had left drying before she went out.
There was straw she could make into a bed. There was a hearth. There was water, if she could lift the jug without spilling it. She knew where all these things were.

She cleared a space beside the hearth with her foot. Yesterday she had left a low basket there, a folded cloth inside it, ready for a baby. Now she looked at its narrow opening and at the delicate ends of his wings. She set the basket on the table instead. The first thing she had prepared for him was already wrong.
She lowered the bundle onto the straw and drew back the top fold.
His eyes found her immediately.

Elara sat on the floor beside him. She was too tired to light the fire yet, too tired even to be frightened with the same force. She placed a finger near his foot. His claws closed around it, awkwardly, without hurting.
Outside, someone called to a neighbour.
She turned towards the door.
Then she looked back at the little claws curled around her finger, and began to understand how much she would have to hide.

chapters.title: The Grave She Invented
paragraphs: The first person to ask about the baby was Nessa.
She had delivered children in half the houses along the lane and sat beside the sick in the other half. Elara knew the small leather bag she carried almost as well as she knew the woman's face.

Elara had stepped outside only far enough to pull the door shut behind her. She needed to look down the lane, to know whether anyone had seen her return. The child had fallen asleep, and for the first time since the mountain she could put both hands against her own body and feel how badly they shook.
Nessa saw the change at once.
“Are you feverish?” she asked. “Any pain beneath your ribs?”
Elara shook her head. Her exhaustion seemed too large to divide into separate complaints.
Nessa stopped with one foot on the packed snow. Her eyes went to Elara's waist, then to the door. Marda, walking beside her, followed the glance.
“You've had him.”
On the slope she had imagined a simple sentence, one that would place her safely inside an ordinary grief. Now that someone was waiting for it, the words would not come.
Nessa took a step towards her.
“Where is the baby?”
Elara put a hand behind her, flat against the door.
“He died.”
The two women became very still.

For an instant she heard the sentence as they must have heard it. A small, terrible piece of news delivered by a woman standing alone in the cold. Nessa's face changed. The curiosity left it so quickly that Elara nearly took the words back.
“Oh, my dear.”

Nessa reached for her arm. Elara let her take it. The woman's fingers were warm through the cloth, and the pressure of them made her aware of how long it had been since anyone had touched her without needing something.
She wanted to lean into that kindness.
Then a faint sound came from the other side of the wood.
Elara coughed.
“Where?” Marda asked.
Elara looked at her.
“Where did you put him?”
Nessa's hand tightened. “Marda.”
“Someone should have helped.”
“In the mountains,” Elara said.
She saw the cave as she spoke, the patch of snow at its mouth and the little wing stretched across the stone. She could have made the lie true by continuing down the path. The knowledge sickened her.
“You buried him there?”
Elara nodded.
Marda looked beyond her at the door, then back at her face. “Alone?”
“I couldn't bear to have anyone there.”
It was the closest she had come to the truth, and it brought tears to her eyes. Nessa mistook them, as Elara had needed her to. She moved closer and tried to draw Elara away from the door.
“Come and sit with us. You shouldn't be on your own.”
“I need to sleep.”
“Then let me come in and make the fire.”
“No.”
The sharpness of it stopped Nessa.

Elara saw the hurt before the older woman concealed it. She had offered something useful, a task for her hands when there was no answer to what had happened, and Elara had refused it as though it were an intrusion.
“Please,” Elara added. “Just for now.”
Nessa released her arm.
“For now,” she agreed.
Marda shifted the basket on her arm.
“You can't stay in there without eating.”

She took out a heel of bread wrapped in cloth. Elara recognised the cloth: she had turned its frayed edge under and stitched it for Marda the previous winter. The stitches were still holding. It seemed impossible that those afternoons belonged to the same village in which she was now afraid to open her door.
“I have some,” Elara said.
“Then have more.”
Marda pushed it towards her. Elara had to lift her hand from the door to take it. She did so slowly, listening for the click of claws on the boards behind her.
“Thank you.”
“I'll fetch the cloth later.”

It was said without threat. That made it worse. A debt as small as a cloth could bring someone to her door when she was not ready. Elara nearly offered to return it at once, then saw Nessa watching her and folded it around the bread instead.

Elara tucked the bread against her side and put her free hand back against the door. Marda did not move immediately. Her gaze travelled over the damp hem of Elara's dress, the snow at the threshold, the hand on the wood. Elara made herself leave it there. Snatching it away would mean something. Everything seemed capable of meaning something now.
At last Nessa turned towards her companion.
“Let her rest.”
They went down the lane together. Marda looked back once. Elara lifted her hand as though saying goodbye, then used it to reach for the latch.
Inside, the baby was awake.

He lay with his head raised above the straw, listening towards the door. When she came into view, his wings lifted and settled. He tried to get up too quickly, tipped forward, and caught himself with both forefeet.
“Quietly,” she whispered.
He did not understand. He came towards her with all the certainty he possessed.

She knelt and stopped him before he reached the cold strip of floor beside the threshold. His body was warm against her fingers. Alive. She had just stood outside and accepted sympathy for his death while he waited a few feet away.
Elara sat back on her heels.

She set the bread on the table and laid the wrapping beside it. She could still unbar the door. She could call Nessa back, begin with the lie and let the older woman see what she had been unable to describe. Her mind made a picture of it: Nessa kneeling here, reaching for the little wing, telling her how to feed him.

Then she remembered Marda asking where she had buried him. There would be no keeping Nessa's discovery between two women for long, even if Nessa wished it. Someone would notice another visitor, another trip for food. She was imagining one kind person where there would soon be a lane full of people.
The baby tried to climb onto her knee. She steadied him, still looking at the door.

If she told them now, they would remember the lie before they looked at him. Every explanation would have to pass through it. She had made that choice in a moment, and already it was closing other ways out.
The baby pushed his head beneath her hand.
She stroked him, carefully following the direction of the scales.
“You mustn't go near the door.”
He pressed harder against her palm.
She could not teach him a door by naming it. She got up, found a folded cloth, and laid it farther from the draught. Then she lifted him onto it. He immediately tried to follow her again.
On the third attempt she stayed beside the cloth.
That worked.

She laughed under her breath, not because it was funny but because she was too tired to manage anything else. The child had understood one thing with perfect clarity: he wanted her near. Everything she needed him to understand would have to begin there.

As the fire took hold, Elara watched the little body settle. She had expected a child who would fit the things she already knew how to do. Wrap him, feed him, hold him. There were parts of that knowledge she could still use, but each one came with a question she had not expected.
How close could he lie to the fire? Did the dry air hurt his wings? Why did he keep opening his mouth and searching beneath the edge of the shawl?
When she bent over him, he caught at her sleeve with sudden urgency.
She knew that need, at least.
“You're hungry.”
She looked towards the shelf where she kept her food.
Outside, the women's voices had faded. The lie had bought her some time. She had no idea how much.

chapters.title: What He Needed
paragraphs: He would not feed as a human baby would.

She had settled him against her body, then tried a few drops of milk on the tip of a spoon. He smelt it without interest and went back to worrying the edge of her sleeve. Elara put the spoon down. Everything she had been told to expect ended there, with a hungry child turning from the one thing she had thought she could give him.
After that she offered him whatever she had.
She softened a piece of bread and held it near his mouth. He smelt it, opened his jaws, and gave her a moment of such foolish hope that she began to smile. Then he turned his head away.
She tried a smaller piece.
He pushed it aside with his nose.
“You haven't even tasted it.”

The complaint sounded so ordinary that for a moment she forgot to be afraid of him. She might have been speaking to any stubborn child. Then he opened his mouth again, and she saw the narrow points of his teeth.
She took her fingers out of the way.
He made the hungry sound, louder this time.

Elara looked from him to the shelf. There was food there, but not much that differed from what she had already offered. She moved between the shelf and the floor, trying one thing and then another. He investigated everything. Nothing held his attention long enough to swallow.
When she brought water, he lowered his face too far into the shallow bowl. He recoiled, snorting, and splashed her sleeve.
She laughed before she could help it.
The little head tilted towards the sound.
“Yes. Very dignified.”

She wiped the water from his nose with the edge of a cloth. He caught it in his mouth. For one alarming moment they pulled against each other; then she stopped pulling, and he let it go. The cloth came away with tiny holes in it.
Elara turned it over.
He watched her fingers rather than the cloth.
She had been thinking of him as something fragile because he was small. He was fragile. He was also equipped with teeth that had passed through woven linen as easily as her needle.
She folded the damaged corner out of sight and put the cloth beyond his reach.
The morning passed in small failures.

There were ordinary tasks she had not expected to find difficult. Getting up from the floor. Carrying water without clutching her belly. Bending to retrieve the bowl after he pushed it under the stool. Each time he called, she forgot how much standing would hurt until she was halfway upright.

At last she pulled the stool close to his cloth and sat before lifting him. He settled more easily that way. She tucked her feet under the seat, supported his breast on one arm and offered the water with the other. He lapped at the surface, badly at first, then with a quick, precise movement of his tongue.
“Yes. There.”
She stopped tilting the bowl before it overflowed. He drank again. It was a small success, but she was so grateful for it that she let him wet the front of her dress without complaint.

Her own hunger became a dull pain. She ate standing up, hurriedly, feeling guilty because he watched. When she offered him part of what was in her hand, he refused that too. His body seemed to have a certainty hers lacked. He knew what the food was not. He could not tell her what it should be.
At last she sat with him on the floor and stopped trying.

He climbed partly into her lap. She supported him without looking, one hand beneath his chest, and rested her head against the wall. The warmth of the fire reached her cheek. She could feel him breathing through her palm.
For a little while he was quiet.
She thought he might sleep. Instead, his head lifted abruptly, and he turned towards the window.
Someone was passing outside.
Elara heard boots, the creak of a basket handle, a greeting called farther down the lane. The baby slid from her lap. She caught him before he reached the strip of light on the floor.
“No. Here.”
He strained against her hands. His nose moved rapidly. He was not looking towards the sound now; he was following something she could not see.
Elara lifted her head and breathed in.

Beneath the smoke from the hearth came a faint, familiar smell. Meat. Not much, only what the air had carried from outside, but enough that she recognised it when she stopped trying to understand the creature and simply noticed what had changed.
She looked at his teeth again.
“Is that it?”
He turned back towards the window.

It seemed obvious once she had thought it. She had wasted the morning offering him her own food because he was hers, because everything about caring for him began with the assumption that he would need what a human child needed.
She went to the shelf once more, although she knew there was no meat on it.

The baby followed her to the edge of his cloth. This time she noticed him stop there, glance towards her, then take one more step. She could not decide whether he had remembered being carried back or merely wanted to be sure she was watching.
She returned him gently.
“I have to find you something.”
She checked the little money she had, moving the coins across her palm. The problem was not difficult to calculate. She could buy a small amount. If he would eat it, she would have to buy more.
His needs would not end because her money did.

She laid out the coins in two little rows. One for fuel. One for food. Taking a coin from the first row made the second look less hopeless until she glanced at the hearth. The wood there would last no longer because she had changed its money into meat.

There were scraps the butcher might sell more cheaply. She had seen them set aside for dogs. The thought shamed her, then angered her: he did not know what a dog was or what she thought a baby ought to eat. If scraps would nourish him, she would ask for scraps. She would have to learn the price before she could afford pride about it.

Elara sat beside the hearth with the coins in her fist. Heat entered the metal slowly. She thought of Nessa's invitation, the offer to make the fire, the kindness she had sent away. She could ask for food. Someone would bring broth, bread, the soft things given to a woman after childbirth. She would have to be grateful for food he could not eat and hide him whenever the person returned to collect the bowl.
A scratching sound brought her back to the floor.
He had found a loose strand in the straw and was worrying at it with his claws. When he saw her looking, he abandoned it and opened his mouth in a hopeful little movement.
Not a snarl. An expectation.
“I know.”
She laid the coins on the table and began looking around the room.

She could not spare the useful things. The pot, the jug, the bedding. She could sell something and need it again before the food it bought was gone. Her gaze passed over each object, weighing the trouble of its absence.
Then she looked towards the place where she kept the small gold keepsake.
She did not go to it immediately.

She made sure the fire was safe. She moved the water where the baby could reach it without tipping it onto his bed. She covered the draught beneath the door. Tasks that could be finished, each providing a short delay before the decision she already understood.
When there was nothing left to arrange, she took out the little wrapped object.
Gold caught the firelight between her fingers.
The baby raised his head.
“Stay here,” she said, and heard how easily the words had begun to belong to her.

chapters.title: The Keepsake
paragraphs: The gold had kept its colour through everything.

It was a small brooch, its pin bent slightly where she had once caught it on a door. She tested the fastening with her thumb. It closed, though not quite as neatly as it used to. Buyers would notice that. They would notice everything except the reason she had kept it wrapped instead of wearing it.

Elara turned it in her hand. Light caught one worn edge, then another. She remembered a hand closing her fingers around it, the warmth of a thumb across her knuckles. At the time she had laughed at the seriousness of the gift. She could remember the laugh more clearly than the words that had prompted it.
Now she could not summon the sound without pain.
The baby shifted in the straw behind her.
She closed her fist.

Before leaving, she knelt beside him. He was watching her closed hand, perhaps hoping that whatever she had been considering so intently might be food. She put the gold on the table and opened her empty palm in front of his nose.
“I'll be back.”
He touched it with his snout.
She said it again because saying it steadied her. Then she put the gold inside her clothing, checked the fire once more, and went out before she could find another reason to stay.
The village had gone about its work while her room became another world.

People carried fuel, shook snow from their boots and argued over ordinary prices. Elara found herself listening to the arguments with a kind of envy. Someone thought a piece of cloth too dear. Someone else had been given less than they asked for. There were quantities people agreed existed. There was a way to say what they needed.
At the meat stall she waited until the person ahead of her had finished.

The smell reached her before she got to the board. Stronger here, edged with cold iron and the fatty scent that clung to the wood. She looked at the pieces laid out and imagined the small head lifting at her window.
“What will you have?” the butcher asked.
She placed the gold on the board.
He looked at it without touching it.
“I need meat,” she said.
“For that?”
She nodded.

He picked it up. She watched his hands and wished she had not. He turned it to inspect the surface, rubbed a mark with his thumb, held it nearer the light. It was sensible work. He could not give her food merely because the thing meant something to her.
Still, she wanted to tell him to be careful.
“How much?” he asked.
“Whatever it will buy.”
His eyes came up to her face.

She had made herself easy to bargain with. She knew it as soon as she spoke. She nearly told him to keep whatever he thought fair, so she could take the food and leave before the absence at home became unbearable.
He began setting pieces aside.
Elara could not tell whether he was being fair. She knew the ordinary cost of food, but not the weight of gold. Each time he added another piece, she tried to imagine how many meals it represented.
He reached for the wrapping.
“Wait.”
She pointed at the heap beside his cutting board, the pieces too small and uneven to display.
“Those as well.”
“You don't want those.”
“Why?”
He looked at her, surprised to be asked. “They take cleaning. There's little enough on them.”
“Then you won't miss them.”

For several seconds his hand remained on the edge of the cloth. Elara had no further argument ready. She could see the vein across his wrist, the little white scar on his thumb. At home her child was waiting for her to do better than stand here and weep over a brooch.
The butcher swept the usable scraps into a separate wrapping. He kept the pieces with sharp chips of bone on his side of the board.
“Cook those in a pot,” he said. “Stretch them out.”
She did not correct him. Relief made her knees shake. She had asked for something and been given it; that was more than she had managed a moment earlier.
She did not know how much her son could eat.

When the butcher wrapped the meat, the bundle was heavier than she expected. She received it with both hands. He moved the gold away from the place where she had put it, and that small change finished the exchange.
Elara turned before he could see her cry.
She had got halfway home when someone said her name.

Nessa stood outside a doorway, Marda beside her. The two women looked first at Elara's face and then at what she carried. For a moment Elara felt the shawl around the baby again, the careful way she had supported his body on the mountain.
This bundle was cold.
“That's a great deal,” Marda said.
Elara tightened her grip.
“You should have let us help you,” Nessa said. “Have you eaten today?”
“A little.”
“And all that is for you?” Marda asked.
The question hung between them. Elara could not pretend not to have understood it.
“I've been weak,” she said. “Since the birth. I need to eat properly.”

Nessa's expression softened at once, but Marda continued looking at the bundle. One corner of the wrapping had darkened where moisture was coming through. Elara shifted it so it would not touch the wool of her shawl.
“Of course,” Nessa said. “Go and get warm.”
Elara thanked her.

It hurt to use their pity this way. She had thought the lie would be something she said once and endured in silence. Instead, she was having to offer it again, to take it out whenever another truth threatened to show.
By the time she reached her door, her arms ached.
She heard him before she opened it.

The cry had become hoarse. It stopped when the latch moved, replaced by the scrape of claws across the floor. Elara pushed the door only far enough to get through and kept a foot against the gap until she had closed it again.
He was there, his wings half lifted, all his attention fixed on what she carried.
“I know. Give me a moment.”
For the first time he did not want her hands, her sleeve or the sound of her voice. He wanted the bundle with a concentration that made him look less helpless and more strange.
She put the meat beyond his reach and cut off a small piece.
He took it so quickly that she flinched.
Then it was gone.
Elara stared at him. He stared at her empty fingers.
“That was it?”
He made an impatient sound.

She gave him another piece, laid on a shallow dish this time. He ate it. Then another. He was clumsy with the dish, precise with the food. She watched the movement of his jaw and the way his throat worked, learning something she would need to remember.
The relief was so great that she began to laugh.
“You could have told me.”
He lifted his face, and for a moment she thought he was smiling. It was only the shape of his mouth. She knew that. She reached for another piece anyway.

When at last he stopped, his body had acquired a roundness that was almost comic. He sat back, blinked at her and lowered himself with enormous care, as if the meal had made him unfamiliar to himself.

Before sitting down, she divided what remained. A portion for the next feeding, another for later, the scraps to be trimmed and examined. She put them in the covered crock on the cold stone beneath the window, away from the hearth and his searching nose. It was less than she had hoped, more than she had possessed when she left.
He watched her shut the lid and made a soft complaint.
“You cannot still be hungry.”
His eyes followed her hands. She showed him both palms, empty, and sat. Only then did he leave the crock alone. Perhaps what he had wanted was not another mouthful after all.
Elara wiped her hands on a clean corner of the cloth.
He rested his head across her knee.
The empty wrapping lay on the table. She knew how little meat remained in the crock beneath the window. Later she would have to think about that.
Now the child was full.

She touched the empty wrapping where the brooch had been. The little stone pendant on its cord still hung beneath her collar; she had not offered it because it would have bought nothing. She let go of the cord and laid her hand on the warm scales of his neck.
He slept before she had finished the first stroke.

chapters.title: A House Too Small
paragraphs: Elara discovered that he liked to sleep with something of hers beneath his head.

At first it was the shawl. If she drew it away, he woke and followed. She tried leaving a folded cloth instead. He inspected it, rejected it and crossed the floor after her, dragging one corner of the shawl in his mouth.
“You can't have all of it.”
He sat on the corner.
Elara looked at him. He looked back with the grave patience of someone certain that the matter had been settled.
In the end she sat near the hearth and let him keep the part that lay across her feet.
The arrangement lasted until his weight began to make her feet go numb.
She named him on an evening when he was still small enough to turn beneath the stool.

The fire had settled low. He lay beside it with his nose on the hearthstone, watching a red point glow beneath the ash. When Elara moved the poker, the point brightened. He lifted his head. She waited, moved it again, and watched his whole attention follow the light.
“Ember.”
He did not look round.
She tried the name again, this time with her hand held out. He abandoned the fire immediately and came to see what was in it. Nothing. He examined her empty palm twice before leaning against it.
“It wasn't an offer of supper.”
He closed his eyes beneath her thumb.

She had tried other names silently, human names she had once imagined calling across a room. None had felt quite his. This one belonged to the small warm creature resting against her wrist, to something she could keep alive if she was careful. She said it once more, quietly enough that only the two of them could hear.

She could not have said precisely when the change began. She noticed it in separate inconveniences. The straw needed spreading farther. His tail reached the leg of the stool. She moved the water bowl, then moved it again when he knocked it over by turning towards her voice.
There were nights when she went to sleep with one image of him and woke to another.
On one of those nights she dreamed of smoke.

She was back in the cave, but its entrance was the doorway of her house. Someone had set the little basket in the snow. She reached for it and found her hands tangled in the shawl, unable to open the folds. Heat drove tears from her eyes, although the ground beneath her feet was frozen.
She woke with a cry caught in her mouth.
The room was quiet. The hearth was low. Beside her, a pale head rose from the dark.
“Ember,” she breathed.
The name brought him to her side.
He pushed his nose beneath her hand.
She caught at him too hard. He recoiled, and she released him at once, horrified by the pressure of her own fingers.
“I'm sorry.”
She showed him her open palm.
He considered it. Then he came back.

Elara laid her hand gently on his face. The scales had become larger, less like a fine pattern on skin and more like overlapping pieces that each caught the light. She followed their edges with her thumb until her breathing slowed.
“I'm here,” she whispered. “It wasn't happening.”
He blinked.
She stayed awake long after he slept again.
In the morning he tried to get himself into the tub.

Elara had fetched water and set the basin where there was room to work. She turned away for a cloth. By the time she turned back, Ember had one forefoot inside, the other balanced on the rim, and an expression of considerable purpose.
“Wait.”
He put his weight on the rim.
She caught the tub before it overturned. Water ran across the boards and beneath her boot. Ember stepped back, surprised by the sudden emptiness where the water had been.
Elara closed her eyes.
He nudged her elbow.
She looked at the puddle, the emptying tub and the creature who had caused it. Then she laughed until she had to sit down.
Ember waited beside her, evidently willing to begin again as soon as she was ready.
This time she held the tub steady. She guided his feet one at a time and stopped him when his wings threatened to follow them into the water. He settled with his tail draped over the edge.
There was very little room left for anything else.
“That was a good tub,” she told him. “Before you found it.”
He lowered his chin, sending water over the rim.

She washed the places he could not reach and learnt where he liked to be touched. The skin at the base of a wing was delicate. The ridges behind his head were not. He leaned shamelessly into the cloth when she rubbed beneath his jaw, then tried to bite the wet end when she moved away.
“Leave that.”
He held on.
She stopped pulling, waited and said his name in a different tone.
His jaws opened.
Elara stared at him.

She tried again with the clean end of the cloth. This time he let it go sooner. The discovery delighted her so much that he became excited too, splashing with his forefeet while she told him how clever he was.
They both ended up wet.

After that she gave the game rules. An open palm meant he could come close. A hand held still, fingers upright, meant he should wait. At first he only waited if she had food. Then he began to pause when she carried the full jug, or when she stooped to put a foot into a boot and had no balance to spare.

She made mistakes too. Once she called him across the room without moving a stool out of his way. He struck it with a wing and hid his head behind the table when it fell. She went to him before picking it up.
“That was mine. I left it there.”

His eye followed the stool when she moved it. She took his face gently between her hands and waited until he looked at her. He was too young to know whose fault anything was, but he could learn whether she would come near him angry.
The next day he stopped at the same place and waited for her to clear the floor. She had to sit down with her face in her hands, laughing, before she could tell him there was nothing in the way.
After another bath, while the cloths dried near the fire, Elara moved the furniture.

The stool went against the wall. The table could turn, though that left less room for her chair. She shifted the bedding and cleared a path between the hearth and the back of the room. Ember followed every movement, putting his head exactly where she needed her hands to be.
“You're the reason I'm doing this. You might help.”
He stepped onto the bedding she had just folded.
She gave up and went around him.

The room changed a little at a time until she could no longer cross it in the dark by memory. Her home was becoming a set of spaces arranged around his body. She put fragile things higher. She kept the door shut even when the air grew close. When he lifted his wings, she watched the beams.
Once, while he slept, she stood at the window and considered the mountains.

She could take him away from the village. The thought was not new. She had been turning it over each time he grew, each time someone paused outside her house. But away was not a place. There was snow, bare rock, and paths where she would be visible for a long way. She had nearly failed to bring him down when he fitted in her arms. Now he could not travel beneath a shawl.
She would have to prepare. Food, shelter, some way of teaching him not to approach every moving thing as though it might be a friend.

On the table she laid a scrap of sacking and began a bundle. The knife, a spare cloth, what was left of the bread. She unfolded it again to take out the knife for his meal. Later she used the cloth to dry the water he had spilled. By evening almost everything was back where it had begun.

Elara sat with the empty sacking in her lap. She had been trying to make a second life out of the things needed to keep this one going. Tomorrow she would ask about the paths beyond the mill. She could do that without explaining why.
Behind her, his claws clicked against the floor.
He had woken hungry.
Elara laid the sacking aside.
The meat was gone again.
She opened the place where she kept the remaining coins, already knowing what she would find. She counted them anyway. Ember waited at her feet, following each movement with interest.
He had no idea that food began anywhere but in her hands.
She looked at the green garment she had made for the cold.

There was work in it that she could measure: evenings of stitching, sections unpicked and sewn again, the careful joining of the fur at the edge. She took it down and held it against herself. It was exactly what she needed for a journey into the mountains.
Ember nudged her empty hand.
Elara folded the garment.

chapters.title: The Price of Warmth
paragraphs: Elara turned the folded cloth so that Nessa could see the stitching.

She had meant to make the offer quickly. Say what she wanted, take whatever money was offered, and leave before the questions began. But now the green fabric lay across her arms, and she found herself smoothing a crease with her thumb.
The fur at the edge had caught a few flakes of snow. She brushed them away.
“Would you give me something for it?”
Nessa looked at the bundle, then at her. Marda remained beside them, watching.

Elara lifted a corner. Pale stitches ran along the border. She knew where she had pulled one too tight and made the fabric pucker. When she had worked on it, she had thought she would undo that section later. There would be time to make it right before she needed it.
Now she hoped Nessa would not notice.
“It's beautiful,” Nessa said.
Elara nodded, too quickly. “I made it.”

Her fingers tightened under the bundle. She could have explained the work, the awkward joins, the way the edging had to be held while the needle passed through. She could have unfolded it properly and shown how much there was. Instead she stood with it pressed against her and tried to remember that she had brought it here to sell.
At home, her son would be hungry again.

The last meal had seemed enormous when she carried it back. He had eaten it, then searched for more. She had laughed at first. Afterwards, while he settled, she had looked around the room for something else she could part with.
There were fewer choices each time.
A gust moved between the houses. She felt it under the shawl at her throat. The folded fabric sheltered her wrists; even here, even now, it was doing the thing she had made it for.
She held it out.
Nessa reached for it, and for an instant they both carried its weight. Elara kept one hand under the lower fold so the edge would not fall into the slush.
“Please keep it dry,” she said.
Then she let go.
Her arms felt foolishly light. She tucked her hands beneath her shawl, but that made it plain she was cold, so she took them out again.

Nessa counted out the money. Elara kept her eyes on the coins because looking at the garment had become too difficult. It was already being held differently, folded over another pair of arms, on its way to belonging somewhere else.
The questions about the meat followed. Already? Had she not bought enough? Was she still so weak?
She gave the explanation she had used before. Recovery. Strength. The child they believed she had lost.
She watched their faces while she spoke. She needed them to believe her long enough to let her go home.
“You don't look stronger,” Marda said.
Elara had no answer to that.
“It takes time,” Nessa said, but she said it while studying her too.
“If you have mending,” Elara said, “I could do it at home.”
Nessa glanced at her hands. “You need rest.”
“I need work that can be done sitting down.”

Marda opened her mouth, then closed it. Elara wondered if she was about to mention the bread cloth Elara had returned, washed and folded. A small proper thing given back, as though she could make herself an ordinary neighbour again by settling that debt.
“There may be linen,” Nessa said. “I can ask.”
“Ask for paid work. Not something to keep me occupied.”
She regretted the sharpness when she saw Nessa's face. But she did not withdraw the request. An hour of pity would not buy the meal after this one.
She also asked about the path beyond the mill. Nessa said the upper track was dangerous after thaw, and the old quarry huts had lost their roofs. Marda wanted to know why she cared.
“I thought walking might help.”
“Then walk where people can see you,” Marda said. “No good comes of being alone all day.”
Elara pressed the coins so hard that their edges marked her palm. The woman meant companionship. Elara heard a watch being set.
Elara dropped the money into her pocket.
“Then I should stop standing in the cold.”
It was almost a joke. Nessa gave her a small, uncertain smile. Marda did not.
At the stall, the butcher recognised her before she spoke.

She placed the coins on the board. There was something worse about their small sound than there had been about offering the gold. The keepsake had bought the first meal. This was what happened afterwards, when a child's hunger continued beyond the gestures a person could bear to call a sacrifice.
The butcher gathered the coins.
“The same again?”
“As much as you can give me.”
He wrapped it. She waited. There was no ceremony this time, only a purchase made by someone who had become a regular customer.

On the way home she shifted the meat from one arm to the other. Her fingers had lost feeling. She could see where the skin had reddened across her knuckles, but the cold itself seemed to have moved deeper, beyond the reach of the shawl.
Ember met her inside the door.
His head was almost at her waist now. She had to turn sideways to get past him. He moved with her, delighted by the smell of the bundle, and knocked the latch against the wall with his shoulder.
Elara caught it before it struck again.
“Careful.”
He stopped.
She looked at him, then at the little mark the latch had left in the plaster. He could listen. He was trying. His body was simply arriving at new sizes faster than either of them could learn them.
She laid out the food. This time she did not laugh when he ate quickly. She sat close enough to slow him with her hand and watched the last of the green garment disappear one mouthful at a time.
When he had finished, she went to the hearth.
She could not thread her needle. Her fingers would not bring the thread to the eye. She tried twice, then put both down before she became angry with something too small to defend itself.

The bundle of sacking was still on the table, flattened beneath the bowl. She added the scraps of linen that could be spared. A journey would be colder without the cloak. Waiting would make Ember larger, hungrier and harder to take through the lane. She wanted a third choice so badly that for a while she sat doing nothing, as if it might arrive while the thread lay unused across her knee.
Ember approached from behind her.

She felt his warmth before he touched her. His head lowered beside her knee, waiting. When she did not move, he settled, crowding the space between the chair and the floor until she had to draw her feet back.
“There's no room,” she told him.
He breathed out against her hands.
She unfolded her fingers.
Warm air passed across the raw knuckles. She rested her palms on the scales beneath his jaw and felt the heat held there. For a while she did not try to sew. He did not try to move.
Outside, boots crunched in the lane. They slowed near her door, then continued.
Elara lifted her head.
The garment was gone. The food was gone. She would be warm enough for the moment if she stayed where she was.
She looked at the empty place on the shelf and began thinking about tomorrow.

chapters.title: Above the Roof
paragraphs: Marda found Father Eldon before she had decided exactly what to tell him.

She began with the meat. The repeated purchases, the amount, Elara's explanation that she needed to regain her strength. Then the closed door, the way she refused visitors. Once she had said these things aloud, they seemed to require something at their centre.
“There is something in that house.”
The priest looked at her.
“Have you seen it?”
“She's hiding it.”
“That is not what I asked.”
Marda drew her shawl closer. “Something is wrong. I can feel it.”

The priest put down the account he had been reading. There were names written on it beside small quantities of grain. Marda could not read all the words, but she knew what it meant when someone carried a sheet like that from house to house.
“People eat badly after a loss,” he said. “They behave strangely. It doesn't give us the right to invent a reason.”
“I'm not inventing the meat.”
“Did she steal it?”
“No.”
“Then you have told me that a woman buys food and closes her door.”
Marda looked towards the lane. He had made her concern sound petty, and she could already imagine the way people would repeat it if he laughed at her after she left.
“If something happens,” she said, “remember I came.”
His expression changed at that. He did not pick up the account again.
He listened to the rest without interrupting. When she had finished, he did not give her the certainty she wanted. She left with her suspicion intact and a new reason to prove it.
Elara first noticed the light on the wall.
It flickered higher than the hearth, bright enough to reach the underside of a beam. She turned with a piece of cloth still in her hand.
“Ember?”
He stood near the open space she had cleared for him. His neck was extended. A narrow breath of flame appeared between his jaws, flared and vanished.
For a moment she could only stare.
Ember turned towards her, pleased by her attention.
“No. Not this way.”
She had spoken too sharply. He jerked his head up. The ridges along his neck struck the timbers above him, and something in the roof gave with a dry crack.
Elara ducked.

Wood fell onto the boards. A gust of cold air entered from above, carrying dust and a little snow. Ember pulled back, startled by the destruction, and struck another loose piece as he tried to fold himself smaller.
“Down,” Elara said. “Lower your head.”
He looked at her through drifting dust.

A gap had opened over him. She could see the night beyond it, a pale, moving patch where the roof had been. He had lifted his head into it. Anyone outside with a clear view of the house could have seen him.
Then a voice sounded in the lane.
Elara ran to the window.
Marda stood outside, looking up.
Marda turned towards the window.
Elara left the window at once. She did not know whether Marda had seen her face, the shape behind her or only the movement of something large above the roof. The woman's next shout answered enough.
“I knew it.”
Ember lifted his wings.
“Against the wall,” Elara whispered. “Low. As low as you can.”

He tried to turn in the space that remained. A claw scraped the floor. She put both hands against his shoulder, guiding rather than pushing; she could no longer move him by force. He folded his wings and lowered himself into the deepest shadow along the wall.

There was a hanging cloth across the alcove where she had once kept her bed, with stacked bedding beneath it. Ember could fold his neck along the back wall, but the curve of one haunch remained outside. She dragged the bedding over that curve and let the cloth hang low over his folded wing. His tail lay along the skirting, partly hidden by the table. From the hearth, a visitor might see only a room crowded with things. Two more steps to the left would undo it.

She lowered the lamp wick. The hearth still gave enough light to enter by; she dared not make the room completely dark. When she looked again, she could distinguish each part of him. She had to hope that someone who did not know where to look would see less.
Someone struck the door.
“Elara.”
She put a finger against her own lips, then laid her palm briefly on Ember's face.
“Still.”
He watched her go.
When she opened the door, Marda tried to look past her. Nessa stood just behind, breathing quickly from the walk.
“Where is it?” Marda asked.
“What do you mean?”
“Don't pretend. I saw it.”
“You saw a shape in the dark.”
Marda pushed forward.
Elara caught the edge of the door. “You cannot walk into my home like this.”
But the opening was already too wide. Marda slipped past her, and Nessa followed with an apologetic look that did nothing to stop what was happening.
Elara closed the door because leaving it open would light the room from the lane.
“The roof is broken,” Nessa said.
“I know.”
“How?”
“Look at the timber.” Elara pointed at the splintered edge. She was offering evidence she did not want them to examine, because it kept their faces turned upwards. “It came down while I was here.”
Marda bent to pick up a piece. The torn fibres were pale and fresh. Elara saw the question forming and spoke first.
“If you brought someone who could mend it, that would be help.”
“You wouldn't let us help before.”
“I didn't ask you to search my house.”
Marda went straight towards the hearth. She bent, looked behind the things near it, lifted a piece of cloth. Elara watched her hands. Somewhere behind her, Ember breathed.
She moved when Marda moved, keeping her own body between the women and the darker end of the wall. It would not conceal him if they went there. It might keep their eyes on her for one more moment.
“Put that down.”
“What are you afraid I'll find?”
“Something that belongs to me.”
Marda turned. Elara met her eyes, though she wanted desperately to look at the place where her son was hiding.
Nessa had begun to look uncomfortable.
Her gaze caught on the edge of the hanging cloth. For a moment she seemed about to reach towards it. Instead, she closed her hand around the strap of her bag.

Marda started towards the table. Nessa moved at the same time, ostensibly to make room for her, and caught the stool with her skirt. Elara heard wood strike wood. Marda turned back, irritated, and began another complaint about the darkness. Nessa remained in the narrow space beside the table, blocking it with her body.
Elara could not tell whether it was clumsiness or a choice. She dared not look at her long enough to ask.
“Perhaps it was smoke,” Nessa said.
“Smoke does not have a head.”
Elara heard a faint movement behind the fabric. She shifted a stool with her foot. The scrape was loud in the small room.
Marda stared at her.
Elara stared back.

The search was hurried and angry rather than thorough. Marda wanted the thing she had seen to be where she expected it, to step into the firelight and prove her right. When it did not, she returned to the argument with Elara. Nessa moved towards the door.
“We should go.”
“I saw it.”
“You've looked,” Elara said. “Now leave.”
For a moment Marda seemed likely to refuse. Then Nessa opened the door, letting cold light fall across the floor, and the choice to remain became harder. Marda backed towards her.
“This has not ended.”
Elara waited until both women had gone before she slid the latch into place.
She stayed beside it, listening to their footsteps. Only when they had faded did she turn.
Ember raised his head. A fold of cloth slipped from a horn. He looked towards the door, then at her, as though waiting to be told whether he had done what she wanted.
Elara crossed the room and put her forehead against him.
“Yes,” she whispered. “You stayed.”
The relief lasted until snow fell through the roof onto her neck.
She looked up.
The repair was awkward, cold work.

Elara could reach the damaged area only with Ember beneath her, his body providing the height she lacked. She steadied herself against the sound timber and told him to remain still. Every time he shifted his weight, the roof seemed to move with him.
“Not yet. A moment more.”

She fitted wood across the opening, using the solid edges rather than the splintered centre to support it. It would keep the worst of the weather out. It would not survive another collision with his head.
Below her, he made a small questioning sound.
“I know. I'm nearly done.”
She looked down through the remaining gap. One pale eye was turned upwards towards her. The sight almost made her laugh, and then the height reminded her not to move too quickly.
When she was safely back on the floor, he lowered his head for her hand.
Elara checked his scales for cuts. She found dust, a little wood caught between two ridges, no injury she could see. She picked the splinter free and held it up.
“The house will lose this argument,” she told him.
He smelt the wood and sneezed.
She laughed then, despite everything.
The laugh faded when she saw the sacking on the table. She went to it and packed again. This time she left the things inside. Even the knife, once she had cut enough meat for morning.

Ember lay across the only clear way to the door. She could step over his tail, but she could no longer imagine leading him through the lane without people seeing him from every window. Before first light, perhaps, when there would be fewer of them. The patched roof ticked in the wind.

She sat on the edge of her bedding with her boots still on. She meant to watch the window until it began to pale. Ember put his head beside her feet, and she rested one hand on him to keep herself awake.
Marda returned to the priest.

This time she had seen something. She described it more than once, using her hands to show its size, its head, the shape that had risen above Elara's roof. Her voice grew louder whenever she came to the part where the house had seemed empty.
Father Eldon let her finish.
“Go home,” he said at last. “There is nothing to be gained by waking everyone in the dark.”
“You don't believe me.”
“At first light,” he said, “we will look.”
Marda stopped speaking.
It was not the answer she had asked for earlier. It was enough to keep her waiting until morning.

chapters.title: The Missing Sheep
paragraphs: Elara heard the accusation before she heard the name.

Something about a sheep. A voice carrying farther than it needed to, repeated by another voice from a different part of the lane. She woke with her cheek against the wall and knew from the light that she had lost the last dark hours. The bundle was still on the table. She had just stood to inspect the patched roof when the first clear words reached her.
“It ate my sheep.”
She stopped beneath the patch and listened.

Ember was beside the hearth. He raised his head at the change in her breathing. The room seemed smaller in the morning light. Every mark he had made in it was visible: the scraped floor, the shifted furniture, the hastily mended place above them.
Elara looked for blood.

She could not make sense of what she saw quickly enough. He had eaten meat. There were stains where she had fed him, marks she had not scrubbed away, things that could be made into evidence by anyone who already believed the accusation. She went to him and examined his face. He leaned into the contact.
“What happened?” she whispered.
He watched her mouth.

There was no answer he could give that would satisfy the people outside. Even if she understood him perfectly, she could not bring them his account of the night and ask them to weigh it against Marda's.
Elara moved to the door.

The voice was nearer now. She could hear Marda calling to people as she passed, telling them what she had seen, what had been hidden, what had been taken from her. The sheep became a creature inside Elara's house. The creature became proof that Elara had deceived them all.
That part was true.

She had lied at the door. She had bought food under a false explanation. She had stood between Marda and the thing the woman had seen. Each lie had protected one day, one meal, one night. Together they now looked like a plan.
Elara put her hand against the latch.

If she opened the door now, perhaps she could speak before too many people came. She could offer to pay for the sheep. She could ask to see what had happened. There must be a difference between losing an animal and deciding that everything strange was evil.
She thought of the coins she no longer had.
Pay with what?

She put the bundle over her shoulder anyway. The strap was a strip of cloth tied at both ends, too short to sit comfortably against her side. She shortened neither end. There would be time to make it comfortable if they got out.
Ember turned at the sight of it. He knew the movement she made before leaving him. He rose so quickly that his back brushed the underside of the table.
“Together,” she whispered. “If we can.”
A man's voice answered Marda farther down the lane. He sounded impatient, almost amused. Marda's reply rose sharply. After a pause, another pair of footsteps joined hers.
Elara eased the window open a finger's width.
“Has anyone found the sheep?” the man asked.
“It isn't in the pen.”
“It could be on the slope.”
“And you could have looked at her roof last night instead of telling me what I didn't see.”

That was not an answer. Elara waited for him to say so. Instead, he asked which way the creature had gone, and Marda began describing its teeth. In the house, Ember rested his chin near Elara's elbow. She closed the window before his breath could mist the opening.

She did not know whether he had taken the sheep. He had frightened her often enough with things she did not know he could do. But nobody outside seemed to want to find the animal now. They were coming to find him.
Elara moved back from the window.

She needed a way to move Ember that did not take him past them. The back of the house offered no simple escape for something his size. The roof had already betrayed them once. If he rose above it now, there would be no doubt left, and she did not know whether he could carry her safely or whether she could make him understand where to go.
She had thought about leaving while there was still time to think. Now thought itself seemed too slow.
Ember came up behind her.

His nose touched the back of her hand. The familiar gesture nearly undid her. He had lived in a world where she was the source of food, shelter and answers. Now he was waiting for an answer she could not find.
“Stay behind me.”
He shifted closer.
“No. A little farther back.”
She showed him with her hands. He took a step, then stopped when she stopped. She wanted to praise him, to make the moment ordinary enough that he would not be frightened by it.
Someone called her a witch.
Ember's head lifted.

The word entered the room with a weight the other accusations had not possessed. A missing sheep could be paid for. A broken roof could be repaired. Elara knew no task that would answer that word once enough people began using it.
She went to the window, keeping to its side.

People were gathering at the front of the house. Not a mass yet, not something without faces. She knew some of them by the things they carried, the sound of their coughs, the way they stood when waiting. People she had passed in the lane that morning she brought the child home.
Nessa was there.

Elara looked for the green garment without meaning to. She could not see it. The absence made her ashamed of where her mind had gone. This was not about the garment. It was about whether Nessa would remember the woman who had made it.
Marda pointed towards the house.
Father Eldon came into view.
The presence of the priest changed how the people stood. The talking continued, but those nearest the door made space. Elara had a brief, painful hope that he had come to quiet them.
Then he called for her to come outside.
“Alone,” he added.

Ember heard the voice and pressed his nose against the strap at her shoulder. She slipped the bundle off and set it by the door. Going out alone meant leaving him in a room that could no longer hold him. Refusing meant letting them decide what the shut door concealed.
Not a request to speak through the door. Not a question about whether she was safe. An instruction given in front of everyone, leaving her refusal to mean whatever they chose.
Ember moved behind her. Wood creaked beneath his weight.
Elara turned.

He had heard the voices. His body had begun arranging itself around the threat: forefeet planted farther apart, neck drawn back, wings no longer folded quite flat. The room could scarcely contain him like that.
She crossed to him before he struck another beam.
“You must listen to me.”
He lowered his face towards hers.
She put her hand where she knew he liked it, beneath the ridge of his jaw. Her fingers found warmth and the faint movement of his throat.
“Whatever happens, you must listen.”
A fist struck the door.
Elara kept her palm against him for one more breath. Then she let go and walked to the latch.
She would have to speak while they could still see her as a woman standing in her own doorway.
She opened it.

chapters.title: At Her Door
paragraphs: They fell silent when they saw him.

The quiet was brief. It held only the scrape of Ember's claws and the sound of Elara's breath. Then someone stumbled back, someone else shouted, and the space before the house seemed to fill with noise all at once.
Elara stepped outside.
“Let me explain.”
Marda pointed past her. “There. You all see him now.”

No one was looking at Elara's face. They were looking over her shoulder, at the pale head that had lowered itself towards the doorway. Ember could not remain in that opening without crowding her. She moved aside just enough to avoid being caught between him and the frame.
The crowd shifted with her.
“Keep back,” she said.
It was meant for both sides.
Father Eldon stood among the people nearest the house. His cross rested against his chest. Elara looked at it because she could not bear the expression with which he was examining her son.
“You brought this here.”
“He was small.”
She heard how foolish it sounded. As though size were the only difference between what they saw and what she knew. As though a smaller body would have made them kinder.
“You told us your child was dead,” Nessa said.
Elara looked at her.
There was injury in the woman's voice. Not yet hatred. Elara reached towards it with everything she had left.
“I was afraid.”
Marda answered before Nessa could. “And you thought we should be the ones to pay for it?”
The sheep again. The creature. The lies. Voices began adding them together. Elara tried to separate the things she could answer, but each reply was drowned by the next accusation.
She would pay for what had been lost. She would take him away. He had not attacked them. Please, they were frightening him.
“Where would you take it?” Eldon asked.
“Away from your houses.”
“That's not a place.”
She had said the same thing to herself at the window. Hearing him use it now made the hope she had assembled from scraps seem childish.
“Up the valley. Let us pass the mill. You can watch us go.”

Several faces turned towards him. She saw how much depended on the next thing he said. A few people had come with their hands empty. One woman kept looking back towards her own door, as if this were an errand that ought already to be over.
“And when it is hungry?” the priest asked. “Whose house will it come to then?”
“I don't know.”
The admission drew a murmur. Elara hurried on.
“I will learn. I've learned everything else without your help.”
“After lying to us.”
“Yes.” She made herself look at Nessa. “I lied because I thought this would happen. I didn't know how to stop it.”

The woman who had glanced towards her door lowered the stick she carried. Someone behind her reached across and pushed it upright again. Elara watched that small correction with a colder fear than any shout had given her.
The heat reached her before she saw the light inside his mouth.

She turned. His lips had drawn back, and an orange glow was rising behind his teeth. The scales beneath his jaw brightened one after another. He was looking over her shoulder at the people gathered outside the house.
Elara stepped into his line of sight.
“Look at me.”
Someone shouted behind her. His gaze flicked towards the sound.
She moved again, keeping herself between his eyes and the crowd. She was close enough to smell his hot breath. It stirred the loose hair against her cheek.

She knew that face. She had wiped scraps of food from the corner of that mouth. She had watched those eyes close when he finally slept. Now she could see the strain of holding still, the small movements of his head as he tried to keep every threatening person in view.
“You mustn't hurt them.”
His throat moved.
She held one hand out behind her, palm towards the crowd.
“No one touch him. Please. Give me room.”

They heard the urgency as proof that he was about to strike. Elara could feel them pressing backwards, feet scraping, a child's voice suddenly raised somewhere beyond the adults. She had to keep her own voice low while every sound around her told him to be afraid.

For one terrible moment she thought he had not understood. She could picture the distance behind her: a few steps to the nearest villager, another row of people beyond. There would be no time to move them. No time to explain that he had been frightened, that they had frightened him.
She raised her hand slowly.
He watched it. His mouth remained open, but the light no longer grew.
“Stay with me.”
She rested her palm against his face.
The contact steadied her enough to feel how badly her other hand was shaking. She curled it against her skirt. He must not mistake her fear for a warning to strike.
Behind her, the shouting changed.
They had seen him listen. She heard it pass from one voice to another: she could command him; the creature obeyed her. What she had hoped would reassure them was becoming another reason to be afraid.
She kept her hand where it was.
If she turned away to answer, would he follow her gaze? If someone pushed past her, would she be able to stop him then?

She wanted to tell them how little he knew. He did not understand their accusation. He understood her voice, a raised hand, the difference between being offered something and being driven back. He was learning the rest from them now.
The glow inside his mouth began to fade.
Elara let out a breath. She had not realised how long she had been holding it.
For a moment she could hear his breathing, the shuffle of feet behind her, the wind moving at the corner of the house. There was still room for someone to speak without shouting.
A young man did.
“He's stopped.”
She turned her head just enough to see him. Dark hair, a short beard, a green cloak pulled close at his shoulder. He was standing apart from those nearest the priest.
“You saw him,” he said. “She told him to stop, and he stopped.”
“Stay out of this,” someone answered.
The young man came forward.

Elara wanted to tell him not to. A sudden movement, the wrong sound, and Ember might undo the very argument the man was making. But he approached slowly, leaving space for her to refuse him. When he raised his hand, it was empty.
Ember watched it.
Elara felt the change beneath her palm. Not calm, not yet, but attention narrowed to something he recognised. She had offered him her hand that way when he was small enough to fit beneath the table.
The young man touched him.
Nothing happened.

His fingers remained near the jaw, away from the eyes and the mouth. He had watched where Elara put her hand. She realised that he was frightened too; the tendons stood out along his wrist. Courage, here, looked like a person taking care not to make a sudden movement.
“Can you keep him still?” he asked her.
“If they stop coming at him.”
The young man looked over his shoulder. “Then stop.”
No flame. No bite. Ember held still and let the unfamiliar fingers rest against his scales.
Elara looked at Nessa.

For a moment she believed this could be enough. Everyone had seen it. There was a man beside her child who had come close without threatening him and remained unharmed. They did not have to believe Elara's account of the quiet evenings in her house. They had proof in front of them.
The priest's voice cut across the silence.
“You would stand with her?”
The young man kept his hand where it was.
“I'm standing here.”
Someone caught his arm.

The movement was sudden enough that Ember jerked his head. Elara pressed against him at once, speaking his name, trying to pull his attention back before the crowd could turn another startled movement into an attack.
When she looked again, the young man had been forced away from her side.
He was still arguing. She could see his mouth move. But the space he had opened had closed, and the people nearest her were no longer waiting to be persuaded.
Elara looked towards the gap in the crowd where he had stood.
Beyond it, a man was bringing a rope.

chapters.title: The Rope
paragraphs: Bram fed the loose end through his hands as he came.

Elara had seen him lead an unwilling animal to market with the same patient movements. There was nothing hurried about him. He watched Ember's head, judged the distance to the doorway, and made a loop.
“Put that down.”
He did not look at her.
Father Eldon moved aside to let him pass. Others followed the priest's example, opening a narrow passage which had not existed when Elara asked to leave.
She stepped into it.
“You can't hold him with that.”
“Then tell him to be still.”
“What will you do when he is?”
Bram glanced towards the priest. Elara followed his look.
“Hold it until we decide,” Eldon said.
“Decide what?”
“What keeps everyone safe.”

She waited for him to include the two lives in the doorway. He did not. Bram was already drawing more rope through his hands, widening the loop. He understood the order well enough to carry it out; only Elara seemed to be asking what would happen afterwards.

She looked from Bram to the rope. They believed in her power when it served them. When she told them her son would not hurt them, she was a liar; when they wanted to put a noose round his neck, she was a witch who could command obedience.
Behind her, Ember made a low sound.

She turned before it grew. He was pushing towards her through the doorway, trying to close the distance Bram had made between them. A shoulder struck the frame. Wood split with a crack that sent the front of the crowd backwards.
“Stay back!” Elara cried.

Ember drew away from the broken timber. The movement caught his wing against the remaining jamb, and he pulled again, frightened now by the house itself. One of the boards tore loose. Dust fell from the lintel.
“Give him room.”
No one seemed able to understand that she was asking them to save themselves.

She moved sideways, out of the opening. Ember followed, folding himself awkwardly through the damaged frame. His claws struck the frozen ruts outside. He lowered his head to her, and for an instant there was only the relief of being able to reach him.
Then Bram threw the rope.
It struck a ridge above Ember's shoulder and slipped. He recoiled, catching the loose loop with a foreleg. Bram hauled before it could fall free.
Ember's cry was sharp enough to hurt Elara's ears.
She caught the rope in both hands.
“Let go!”
Bram pulled harder. The fibres burned across her palms. She could see the loop tightening above the dragon's foot, where the scales were smaller and moved with the joint.
