She stopped pulling against Bram. Instead she tried to lift the turn of rope away from Ember's leg, but his foot would not stay still. He was looking down at the thing that hurt him, and the light had begun to gather in his throat again.
He could end this. The knowledge came without permission.
One breath. Bram would release the rope. The people behind him would run. No one would stand between them and the lane.

Her hands were trapped between the tightening fibres and a body too strong to hold. She loosened one finger, then another, afraid he would pull away and take the skin with him. Bram could see that. She was close enough to know he could see it, and still he hauled.
“You're hurting him.”
“Stand clear.”
As if her place in this were the only thing wrong with it.
Elara saw Nessa's face beyond Bram's shoulder and hated herself for having thought it.
“No,” she said. “Look at me.”
Ember's gaze found hers. The rope jerked. He cried again, but the fire did not come.
Another man seized Elara from behind.

Her fingers slipped from the rope. She tried to twist out of his grip and felt her shoulder wrench. The pain blinded her for a moment. When she could see again, Ember had reared, dragging Bram a step through the mud.
The man holding Elara swore and let go so that he could get out of the way.
Bram lost his footing. He released the rope to save himself, and Ember tore his leg free of the slackening loop. A narrow red line marked the pale scales.
People were shouting for weapons now.
The young man in the green cloak tried to come forward again, but two others held him back. Elara saw him push against them. He could not reach her. She could not wait for him.
She put herself beneath Ember's lowered head.
“You have to go.”

She tried the movement she had taught him in the room: a hand held upright, a step backwards to make space. His eyes went to her fingers. For a moment he seemed almost relieved to be given something he knew how to do. He stopped coming towards her.

She would have to ask for something else now. Something for which there had been no game beside the hearth, no reward held out when he got it right. He was looking to her for the familiar end of it, the open palm that would bring him close again.
His breath struck her hair. He pressed his muzzle towards her breast, seeking the place where he had always fitted, and nearly knocked her down. She braced herself against him.

There was nowhere in the village large enough to hide him. The house had been too small before Bram broke its last promise of safety. There was nowhere she could run with him that the crowd would not follow.
But above them the sky was empty.
She looked at his wings.
He had opened them in the house and frightened himself against the beams. He had never had all the room he needed. Now the people nearest their pale, folded edges were backing away.
“Up there,” she whispered.
He followed her face, not her pointing hand.

She wanted to climb onto his back. She could imagine it so clearly that for a heartbeat it felt possible: her arms round his neck, the ground falling away, every voice below reduced to something the wind could carry off.
Someone caught her skirt. She stumbled, and a hand fastened round her wrist.
Ember's mouth opened.
“Don't.”
She had to say it to him again. She would have to keep saying it until he was beyond their reach.
“Fly, Ember.”
He crouched towards her. One wing opened, striking the broken edge of the doorway; the other spread over the crowd. People ducked. The hand at Elara's wrist loosened.
She pushed at his chest with both palms.
It was a ridiculous little force against all of him. Yet he moved away from it as he had moved away from the washcloth, the hearth, the table she had told him to leave alone.
“Go on. You can do it.”
His wings lifted.

The first downward stroke threw dust and scraps of straw against her face. He rose badly, one foot slipping in the mud, and landed hard enough to shake the ground. A shout of triumph came from behind her.
Elara lifted her arms, cried out at the pain in her shoulder, and clapped her hands once above her head.
He looked at her.
“Again.”
This time he pushed with his hind legs. The great pale membranes caught the air, and his claws left the earth. His wounded foot curled against his chest. The next stroke lifted him above the eaves.
Elara laughed once, a broken sound she could not have stopped.
He turned towards her immediately.
“No. Keep going.”

Someone dragged her backwards. She fought to remain where he could see her, arm extended, pointing towards the mountains. His body hung against the low clouds, awkward and beautiful. Every part of her wanted to call him down.
She made her mouth say the other thing.
He climbed.

A stone passed close to his wing. Another struck the roof and rolled into the lane. Elara scarcely felt the hand twisted in her hair. She was watching him clear the houses, watching the wings that had so often filled her kitchen find their proper shape.
He looked back.
She was certain of it, though she could no longer see his eyes.
She raised her empty hand until they forced it down.

chapters.title: The Stone
paragraphs: Without him, the space outside the house seemed enormous.
Elara was on her knees. One palm rested in the rut his claw had made. Water was seeping into it, turning the disturbed earth black.
For a moment she could think only that the ground had begun to thaw.
Then Marda caught her chin and made her look up.
“Your son ate my sheep.”
Elara knew there ought to be an answer. She had offered one before: work, payment, departure. Now the words seemed to belong to a conversation that had ended while she was looking at the sky.
“I'll go,” she said.
“He has gone.”
Marda spoke as though Elara had arranged an escape for a thief and remained behind to enjoy the joke.
Elara looked past her. The strip of sky between the roofs was empty.
Good, she thought. Farther. Keep going.
Father Eldon approached. His robe brushed the muddy water at the edge of the rut. She watched the dark patch spread through the hem.
“You had your chance to tell us.”
“Would you have let him live?”
It was not defiance. She wanted him to answer. If there had been another way, if she had been foolish enough to miss it, she wanted to know what it was before the hands behind her tightened again.
The priest looked towards the broken doorway.
“See what you have brought upon us.”
She saw the board hanging from one nail. Beyond it, the edge of the table. A scrap of pale cloth on the floor which she had used to wipe Ember's mouth.
“Let me leave.”
“You can be heard,” Eldon said, “when you stop making demands.”

She looked up at him. Her mouth was dry enough to hurt. Behind him, the lane remained open in the direction she needed to go. Only people stood in it. She had spent so long trying to solve the problem of getting Ember through wood and stone that she had forgotten a person could move aside and choose not to.
“Then hear me. No one needs to touch me. He has gone. I will go too.”
“And bring it back?” Marda asked.
“You could shut your door. You could let me walk past it.”

Marda shook her head, not violently but with the weary certainty she had once used about weather. Elara remembered her pushing bread into her hands. She had eaten it. For part of a morning it had helped keep her upright. She could not make that kindness fit the woman now refusing to let her stand.
Someone in the crowd laughed.
The young man was still there. She caught sight of his green cloak between two shoulders. He was speaking, trying to make himself heard. When he took a step towards her, the men beside him closed in.
“She hasn't hurt you,” he called.
“Ask her about the sheep, if that's what you came for. Ask where she means to go. What is this?”

He spoke more quickly as nobody answered. A man beside him told him to lower his voice. Elara heard the absurdity of it with painful clarity: the person asking them to stop was the one being told to be calm.
An answer came from elsewhere. Elara could not make out the words, only the anger with which the crowd took them up.
A hand held something out to the priest.

She looked at it without understanding. A stone, grey on one side and brown with wet earth on the other. It had probably lain beside this lane longer than she had lived in the house. She might have stepped over it carrying meat. She might once have moved it aside with the toe of her shoe.
Now everyone near it was watching.
Nessa stood behind the woman who held it. Her lips had drawn inward. She looked at the stone, then at Elara, and lowered her eyes.
“Nessa.”
The name came out very quietly.
Nessa did not answer.

She had opened her bag. Elara saw the pale edge of linen inside it and thought, for one foolish instant, that this meant help was coming. Then another woman looked round. Nessa let the flap fall shut.
“She can hardly stand,” Nessa said.
Eldon did not turn. “We can all see that.”
It was enough to silence her. Elara waited for another sentence, something that made the first one mean she should be allowed to rise. None came.

Elara remembered the green garment laid across her arms, the careful way she had touched the stitching. Her hands had been gentle then. Elara tried to find those same hands in the crowd and could not see them.
Someone called her a witch.
Someone else said the word again, louder.
The first blow struck her shoulder.

She fell sideways against the person holding her and heard a gasp from very close by. It might have been her own. For an instant the crowd seemed shocked by what it had allowed. There was a pause in which she thought it could still stop.

One man stepped back. His heel struck someone else's boot, and he muttered an apology. Elara heard it while she was on the ground: an apology for a boot, easily given. She tried to lift her face towards him, but he was already looking at the priest, waiting to discover what sort of moment this would be.
Then another stone landed beside her knee.
She raised an arm over her head.

The movement was useless. She knew that, yet her body made it. She wanted to cover the back of her neck, to curl away from the feet around her, to find the little space under the table where Ember had once hidden with her shawl in his teeth.
She heard the young man shout. She heard the priest speak. Their words no longer reached her separately.
Above the lane a pale shape moved against the clouds.
No.
She pushed herself up on one hand. Her elbow shook. She could not tell whether the shape was coming closer or merely turning, but she had to make him understand.
“Go.”
No one heard.
She tried again, lifting her face towards the roofs.

The blow that followed knocked her back into the rut. Water ran against her cheek. For a moment she was in the cave again, stone beneath her, cold entering through every part of her clothing. She remembered the cry she had tried to leave behind.
She had gone back.
Whatever else had happened, she had gone back for him.
Her fingers opened against the mud. She wanted his small claw in them. She could almost remember its weight exactly, before he grew too large to hold.
Someone pulled her shoulder. She tried to tell them not to move her yet.
The word would not come.
When the crowd fell quiet, Elara no longer moved.

One of the women bent towards her and straightened without touching her face. A man wiped his hand against his coat. The broken board at the doorway shifted in the wind and knocked, softly, against the wall.
Father Eldon looked at the people around him.
He said the village had been delivered from a witch. He spoke loudly enough for those at the back to hear and claimed the killing as an act that would please God.
No one cheered.
The young man in the green cloak pulled free of the hands that had held him. There was a mark across his mouth. He looked down at Elara, then at the priest.
“She needs a grave.”
“Not in our ground,” Father Eldon said.
The young man stared at him.
“Our families are buried there. You would put her among them?”
Behind the priest, Marda drew her shawl close. Nessa turned away from the body.
The young man knelt. For several moments he did nothing but arrange Elara's arm beside her, moving it with a care that made the people nearest him look elsewhere.
Someone asked what they were to do with her.
The priest pointed beyond the last houses, towards the rough ground falling away into the valley.
“Take her there.”
Across the lane, the loop of rope lay where Bram had dropped it.
No one picked it up.

chapters.title: A Familiar Scent
paragraphs: Above the roofs, before the crowd fell quiet, Ember heard her call once more. Her voice reached him long after he could no longer catch her scent.

Ember turned towards it. Below him the houses tilted, their narrow lanes dark against the snow. He could see movement where he had left her, but too many bodies occupied the same small place. Each time he found her pale face, someone passed in front of it.
He lowered one wing.
Her cry reached him again.
Go.

He knew the sound. It belonged to the pointing hand, to the insistence that made him give up a strip of cloth or move away from a flame. He had resisted it before. She had always waited until he did what she asked.
His wing rose.
The houses dropped behind him.

He flew until the air no longer smelt of people. A ridge lifted out of the cloud ahead, and he reached for it with his feet. His wounded leg failed when it touched the slope. He slipped, wings scraping over stone, then caught himself on the edge of a hollow beneath an overhang.
There he folded into the rock.
For a while he could do nothing else.
His chest moved too quickly. The membranes of his wings trembled against his sides. Whenever he tried to put weight on the injured foot, pain ran up his leg and made his jaw open.
No hand came to examine it.
He lowered his head and touched the sore place with his tongue. The taste was wrong. He tried again, carefully, as she had carefully cleaned the tender skin at the corners of his mouth.
The bleeding slowed.

Outside the hollow, snow blew sideways across the mountain. The little particles struck his face and melted. He moved deeper beneath the overhang, where rock sheltered his back, and drew the wounded foot against his chest.
He had been cold before, but never with so much room around him.

In the house, something had always stopped the cold: a wall, her skirt, a folded piece of cloth she moved closer when he began to shiver. Even when he could not see her, there had been the sound of her shifting on the stool or the soft scrape of a cup against the table.
Here, water ticked from the rock.
He lifted his head each time it fell.

A gust rattled dry stems at the entrance. He moved towards them before he saw what had made the sound, striking his shoulder against the side of the hollow. The pain in his leg flared. He lowered his head among the stems and breathed through them, searching for the scent that should have followed a scrape at a door.
Wet bark. Stone. Nothing familiar.
He backed into the shelter and set his sound foot beside the other one. The wind moved the stems again. This time he watched without rising, though his wings lifted a little from his sides.

Once he made the sound that used to bring her from the doorway. It travelled into the hollow and came back thin and strange. He stopped, listening for the answer she usually gave before he had finished asking.
There was only another drop of water.
He pressed his muzzle beneath the fold of one wing.
There she was.

Faintly, among the smells of his own body, he found wool, wood smoke, the warmth of her skin. She had leaned there when she reached across him. Her hands had rested against the fine scales beneath the wing joint.
He inhaled and held still.
The scent did not tell him where she had gone. It did not make her appear in the opening. But it gave him something he could recognise, and he kept his face close to it until his breathing slowed.
He had waited for her before.

The latch would lift. Cold air would enter first, then the smell of the street, then Elara. Often she carried food. Sometimes she came with nothing, and the absence of a bundle did not matter once she touched him.
He could wait.

He arranged his tail beside his feet. He tucked his head into the curve of his body, leaving one eye turned towards the entrance. Snow gathered beyond the shelter. A dark bird crossed the opening and vanished into the cloud.
His eyelid lowered.
In sleep, the rope tightened again.
He jerked upright so violently that a horn struck the overhang. He bared his teeth at the empty entrance. Heat rose inside him, lighting the rock close to his mouth.
Nothing moved there.
He swallowed the heat and listened.

The people were gone. The hands that had pulled her away were gone. He could not hear them now, but he could feel the moment of the rope closing whenever his leg shifted. He could still see her arm disappear between other bodies.

He saw again the ground falling away beneath his feet, her face turned upwards. He had obeyed the hand pointing him away. Now each time he settled, the same separation opened behind his eyes: Elara below, himself above, too much air between them.
He crawled to the edge of the hollow.
Mist covered the lower slopes. The village was somewhere beyond it, where smoke sometimes rose in small straight lines before the wind broke them apart. He looked for those lines and saw nothing.
His injured foot touched the snow. He drew it back with a soft cry.
Still no answer.
He sank down at the entrance, head between his forelegs. Water gathered at the corner of one eye and ran along the fine grooves of his scales. He blinked against it, then shut his eyes.

In the dark behind them she was sitting on the floor, rubbing him dry with a cloth too small for the work. He had tried to bite the moving edge. She had caught his jaw, not hard, and waited until he released it.
Then she had put her forehead against his.
He moved towards the remembered touch and met the stone beneath his chin.

chapters.title: What She Taught Him
paragraphs: Hunger brought him out of the hollow.

He stood with three feet bearing most of his weight and watched the white slope below. Far off, something small moved between rocks. His head followed it. His body knew how to narrow its attention, how to forget everything except distance and movement.
Then the creature vanished, and he looked towards the valley again.
Food came from there. So did Elara.
He spread his wings.
The left membrane dragged across the rock. He lifted it clear, testing the air as it pressed against the wide, delicate surface. Pain remained in his foreleg, but his wings were sound.
He stepped to the edge.
Below was a drop greater than the height of the house. He looked down, drew back, and turned his head as though she might be standing behind him to tell him what to do.
There was only the hollow, empty except for the marks his body had left in the snow.
He remembered her raised hands.

The sound she had made when he first rose above the roofs had been different from the other sounds. For an instant it had been the voice she used when he put his nose in the wash water, when he carried off a piece of cloth and waited to be followed. A bright sound. He had turned towards it because he wanted it again.
He crouched.
This time the air caught him before his feet began to fall.

He did not climb high. He followed the slope, letting the mountain guide him down. The wind moved beneath his body and held him where the rock no longer could. Each stroke of his wings became less awkward than the last.
The mist thinned.
He saw the village.
For a moment he flew straight towards the houses. Then a memory of the rope checked him. He curved away, circling beyond the edge of the roofs where he could see the lane without entering it.
There was no crowd at the doorway.
The broken wood remained. One pale board leaned against the wall. A person crossed the lane carrying a bundle, glanced upwards, and ran.
Ember descended beyond the last house.

He landed among rough grass, stumbling when his hurt foot took too much weight. Earth clung to his claws. A fence stood between him and the nearest garden; he stepped over it without noticing the way the top rail broke beneath his hind leg.
He stopped before the house.
The smell of it reached him through the shattered opening. Ash, old straw, the greasy scent of meat, damp wool. He lowered his head and breathed them in.
Elara was there in every part of the room.
He pushed his muzzle inside.

The table had shifted. One of its legs lay at an angle. A cup was broken beneath it, the pieces scattered where his feet used to be. He nudged the edge of the tabletop, expecting the movement to bring her out from behind it.
Nothing stirred.

He knew where she slept. He turned towards that place, but his shoulders caught beneath the damaged lintel. He could force them through only by tearing away more of the wall. He stopped pressing forward.
Careful.
It was not a voice in the room. It was the memory of one, joined to her hands guiding his head away from a shelf.
He withdrew.

Beside the threshold lay the bundle she had taken off her shoulder. One corner had torn, leaving a piece of linen in the mud. Ember lowered his nose to it. The cloth carried her hands, the food she had cut, the cold air that came in whenever she opened the door.
He caught it between his teeth and pulled. A knife struck the boards with a sharp sound. He let go at once. The bundle slumped, bread rolling out beside his foot.
He waited for her to pick it up.
He left it where it lay and moved his muzzle along the threshold. Beyond it, the smells of the lane had been churned together by many feet.
From farther down the lane came a shout. A door slammed. Ember turned sharply, and the people who had been watching disappeared behind their walls.
None of them was her.
He returned to the doorway and lowered his nose to the ground.

The smell of many people lay across the mud. Leather, sweat, smoke, the coarse fibre that had closed round his leg. He passed over it too quickly and flinched when the loose end of the rope stirred beneath his breath.
Then he found her.
Not the old warmth in the straw. Something nearer, sharper. Her scent was mingled with earth and the same taste he had found on his injured foot.
He followed it.

At first it led away from the door into the place where the people had stood. He circled there twice, confused by all the crossing trails. Then he found it again beyond the lane, moving towards the open ground behind the village.
His head stayed low.

He passed the last wall. The ground fell into a shallow valley, its winter grass pressed flat by snow. Beyond it rose a slope with old fence posts leaning at different angles. A black bird lifted from one of them as he approached.
He knew her shawl before he knew the rest.
It lay dark against the earth, one edge caught beneath her shoulder. He had slept on that cloth. He had dragged it across the floor and hidden with it under the table until she found him.
He made the little sound that belonged to their doorway.
She did not sit up.
He came closer, quickly now, placing his feet on either side of the patch of ground where she lay. Her hair covered part of her face. One hand rested open beside her.
He brought his muzzle down to it.
Her fingers did not close.

chapters.title: Earth for a Bed
paragraphs: He touched her cheek with the narrow front of his muzzle.
Her head moved against the grass. Nothing else did.

Ember drew back, startled by how easily he had moved her. She had always met his touch with one of her own. Even when she was tired, even when her eyes remained closed, her hand would rise to the place he had offered it.
He lowered himself beside her.
The wind lifted her hair. He watched it move and pressed his nose closer, searching for the small current of air that used to warm the scales around his nostrils.
There was none.
He breathed out over her mouth.
Warmth passed from him to her skin. He did it again, keeping the fire deep inside, where it could do no harm. Her hair stirred beneath his breath. For an instant the movement looked like an answer.
He waited for the rest.
Beyond the broken fence, a crow settled on a post. Its claws clicked against the wood. Ember raised his head and showed his teeth until it flew away.
When he looked down, Elara was still lying in the same position.
He made a sound louder than the one at the doorway. It opened in his chest and rose until the hillside gave it back. He stopped to listen, his head tilted towards her face.
Nothing.

He nudged her shoulder. The movement drew the shawl away from her neck, exposing the small pendant on its cord. He had seen it disappear beneath her dress when she bent over him. Now it lay against her skin without moving.
He touched it with his nose and felt the cold.

Even in her deepest sleep she had moved beneath his weight. He shifted his chin onto her open palm, where the small bones pressed against his scales. He stayed there until he could no longer pretend the wind stirring her sleeve was the beginning of a touch.
At last he stopped calling.

He lay with his body curved around hers, shutting out the wind. His wounded leg stretched beyond her feet. He did not lick it now. He watched her face until the details blurred, then blinked them clear and began again.
She was not merely away from him, as she had been when she walked through the door.
He could smell her. He could touch her. All the distance he had crossed had brought him here, close enough to feel a strand of her hair against his mouth.
Yet he could not reach her.
The light changed on the slope. Meltwater trickled down a shallow groove in the earth and soaked into the cloth beneath her arm.
He lifted his head.
Water was running towards her. He pressed a foot into its path. The trickle divided, found its way round his claws, and continued downhill.
He scraped at the ground.

Dark earth turned beneath the pale grass. He scraped again, making a channel that carried the water away. The work shifted loose soil against Elara's sleeve. He brushed it back with his muzzle, then looked towards the higher ground beside the fence.
The earth there was dry beneath its frozen crust.
He began to dig.
At first he used both forefeet. Pain checked the injured one, and he drew it close to his body, working with the other. Grass tore. Small stones rolled from the place he was opening.

The hole grew unevenly. He circled it, scratching from a new angle, stopping whenever he came too near the place where Elara lay. His tail struck one of the broken rails and knocked it flat. He scarcely noticed.

He had watched her make a place for him out of what she had. A little hollow in the straw. A folded shawl beneath his body. When he grew, she had moved the furniture and laid cloth over the places where the floor was cold.
He could make a place for her.

He dug until the dark opening was longer than her body. The bank on its windward side stood high enough to shelter a small face. He lowered his head into it, testing its depth, then withdrew and scraped away a stone that pressed against his jaw.
She remained where he had left her.
Moving her was harder than breaking the earth.

He caught the edge of her shawl between his teeth, but the cloth tightened beneath her shoulder and drew her head sideways. He released it at once. For a long moment he stood over her, frightened by the result of his own strength.
Then he knelt.
He worked his muzzle beneath the cloth at her back. Slowly, with his head supporting her shoulders and the curve of a folded wing holding her from slipping sideways, he drew her towards the hollow.
Every few inches he stopped.
Her hand trailed in the grass. He caught it gently against the side of his jaw and brought it with the rest of her. The fingers brushed his scales on the way down, and he froze beneath the touch.
For that instant he waited again.
Then her hand fell away.
He lowered her into the earth.

She lay on her back, one side of her face turned towards the open sky. Her hair spread across the dark soil. He nudged the edge of the shawl over her shoulder, covering the place where the wind had reached her.
He could no longer put his body round hers without hurting her. The space was too narrow, his weight too great.
He stayed at the edge instead.
When he moved, loose earth slipped from beneath his foot and fell across the shawl. He watched it settle. Then he pushed another little fall of soil towards her feet.

He paused after each movement, as he had paused when she taught him to take food without catching her fingers. He used the side of his foot, not the points of his claws. Small roots and stones he drew away.

Once a pebble rolled towards the hollow of her throat. He stopped working, reached down and lifted it between the very ends of his teeth. He placed it well beyond the mound. When he returned, his breath made a little cloud above her face and vanished without an answering cloud beneath it.
The earth covered her skirt.
Then her hands.
He stopped before it reached her face.
The wind was quieter inside the hollow. A strand of her hair lay across her mouth. He lowered his head and moved it aside with his breath.
Her eyes did not open.
Something changed in the sound he made then. It was lower than a call, without the rising note that asked for an answer. He held it until there was no breath left to sustain it.
Afterwards he finished the work.

He pressed the loose soil with his muzzle. He drew more earth over the shallow places. When nothing of the grey dress remained visible, he found a broad stone among those he had uncovered and pushed it to the head of the mound.
The stone had no mark on it.
He pressed it deeper until it would not move beneath his nose.
Then he lay down beside it.
The village smoke drifted up the valley. It carried the smells he had followed earlier: hearth ash, meat, damp roofs. Beneath them lay other memories, sharp enough to bring his head upright.
The rope. The hands round her arms. Her face disappearing among the people while he rose into the sky.
He looked at the mound.
He had obeyed her. He had flown where she pointed and left the people unharmed. He had waited for her to come back.
His mouth opened.
This time, when heat gathered behind his teeth, no hand rose to stop it.

chapters.title: The Fire He Kept
paragraphs: The first shadow crossed the market before anyone looked up.
Marda was speaking beneath the butcher's awning. A woman beside her turned towards the sudden change in light, and the words died in Marda's mouth as the shadow travelled over her face.
Ember came down beyond the line of roofs.
His feet struck hard. A stack of empty baskets overturned. The awning snapped in the wind from his wings, and the butcher ducked behind the counter with his knife still in his hand.
For one suspended moment, everyone remained where they were.
The dragon looked from face to face.

Marda stumbled backwards into the woman beside her. Their arms tangled. She pulled free, found the entrance to the narrow lane and pushed towards it without looking to see whether her companion had followed.
A cry went up behind them.
Ember knew that sound. He had heard it outside the house, where the people drew together and showed him their teeth. This time they were drawing apart.
He did not follow the first person who ran.
His gaze had caught on a length of rope hanging from a hook beside the stand.
Heat moved through his chest.

There had always been time before: a warning glow, a breath held while he waited for her voice, the touch that made him fold his anger back inside. His body still knew how to hesitate. He turned his head as though the small pale hand might appear at the edge of his sight.
It did not.
He breathed fire.

The awning caught first. Flame raced across the dry cloth and climbed the wooden supports. The rope blackened where it hung. A bowl burst on the counter, and the people sheltering behind it scrambled away as the hot fragments fell.
Ember stepped towards them.
A man threw a crate in his path. It struck his wounded foreleg. He roared, and the sound drove the man backwards against a wall.
Another breath of flame filled the lane.

Smoke rolled up between the houses, blotting out the pale sky. People who had been running towards one opening turned towards another. A shutter slammed; a moment later the door beneath it opened again, and a woman came out clutching a bundle against her chest.

The village had been built close against the cold. Roofs leaned towards one another. Timber had been stored in narrow yards. Kindling stood beside doors, ready for hands that expected an ordinary evening.
The fire found it all.

At the well, three people reached for the rope together. One pulled before the bucket had filled. Water spilt down the stones as they dragged it up. A woman took it from them, carried it towards the market, and stopped when the heat drove her back. She had meant to save a roof. Now she tipped the water over a blanket and held it across the head of the child beside her.

The child had lost a shoe. He kept trying to turn back for it. His mother caught his wrist and pulled him towards the stream while he hopped and cried, each step leaving one small bare print among the tracks in the soot.

Ember saw none of this as a whole. He saw a hand close on an arm, heard a cry, and turned. By the time his head reached the place, both figures had disappeared behind a wall. Another hand lifted farther off. Another voice struck the air. His anger kept finding shapes that resembled the ones around Elara and losing them in smoke.

Ember moved through the market with his wings held half open. The heat did not drive him back. Sparks struck his scales and vanished, while the people around him covered their faces and crawled beneath the smoke.
Some called for water. Some called for the priest. Others called names which received no answer.
He heard only pieces of them.

At a turn in the lane, he saw a man tugging at a door that would not open. The man's shoulders strained, hands locked round the handle. For an instant the movement became another one: Bram pulling against the rope, Elara's fingers sliding free of it.
Ember turned towards him.
The man saw the light inside his mouth and abandoned the door.
Flame struck the wood. The upper hinge pulled loose with a shriek. Ember jerked his head at the sound, searching through the orange light for the person he remembered.
There was no Elara behind the falling boards.
He moved on.

The fire had its own movement now. It travelled where he had not looked, climbing stairs, crossing beams, entering rooms through the small spaces the wind had always found. He could burn a doorway and leave it, but the flame did not leave with him.

The wind shifted towards the stream. A man who had escaped the first burning lane ran back to close the gate of his yard, as though it might keep the sparks out. He let go when the latch scorched his fingers. Through the open doorway behind him, a row of wooden cups caught light one by one.

He had not been outside Elara's house that morning. He had been repairing a leaking barrel. Now the barrel lay split across his floor, its little store of water sinking uselessly between the boards. He backed away with his burned hand held against his chest, watching the room where he had expected to eat that night.
Behind the market, Nessa pressed herself into a recess between two walls. Marda had gone ahead, coughing, one hand against the stone. Neither woman looked back towards the other.
Across the square someone lifted a bucket, stumbled, and lost most of the water before reaching the burning stand.
Ember turned towards a movement on his left, striking a post with his wing. Part of the awning above it collapsed, and the fall opened a new space beside the market wall.
A young man stood there.
His green cloak was grey with ash. He had one hand raised against the heat, palm towards the dragon.
Ember drew breath.

chapters.title: The Hand He Remembered
paragraphs: The young man did not run.
There was nowhere clear to run to. A burning beam lay across the narrow opening behind him. To one side stood the market wall; to the other, Ember's body filled the space where the awning had been.
The man kept his hand raised.
Ember saw the soot on the palm. He saw the way the fingers trembled without closing. A cut across the man's mouth had opened again, leaving a dark mark at the edge of his beard.
The dragon's throat brightened.
“Easy,” the man said.
The word scarcely carried over the fire.
Ember lowered his head. He was close enough now for the man's scent to separate itself from the smoke: wool, leather, frightened sweat, blood.
And something he knew.

He had stood beside Elara with this person. Not across the lane, not beyond the pull of a rope, but beside her. The hand had come towards him slowly. He had waited for the blow and received a touch instead.
The memory was precise.
Fingers resting on the side of his face. Elara watching. The brief change in her breathing when nothing bad happened.
He looked at the raised hand again.
There was no weapon in it. No loop waiting to close. The man had lifted it against the flame, yet even with the dragon's teeth so near, he had not turned it into a fist.
Ember held his breath.
The heat inside his mouth faltered.
Above them, a strip of burning cloth tore free. It fell between the man and the wall, and he flinched sideways. Ember's head followed the movement.
The man stopped at once.
His fingers rose a fraction, then stopped short of the scales. His hand remained in the narrow space between them, shaking more visibly as he waited.
Slowly, Ember closed his mouth.

The man moved his hand down before trying to move his feet. He did it a little at a time, as Elara did when she took something away that Ember wanted. His gaze stayed on the dragon's face. Ember could see him searching for room beneath the wing, judging the strip of ground between claw and wall.

A coal struck the man's sleeve. He slapped it out, and the sudden sound made Ember's neck tighten. But the hand rose open again. Empty again. The dragon followed it until the heat in his throat eased.
The man let out a breath that became a cough. He bent at the waist, one arm across his face. When he straightened, the dragon was still watching him.
Something in that face had changed.

Fear remained. Ember knew it well enough now. But the man looked at the pale scales streaked with earth, at the wounded foot held awkwardly against the ground, and his eyes moved towards the far end of the village.
He said Elara's name.
Ember lifted his head sharply.
For a heartbeat he searched behind the man.
There was only the wall, blackened by smoke. The sound had brought her close and taken her away again in the same instant.
He made a low, broken noise.
The man's hand sank.
He looked down, and Ember no longer waited for anything from him.
The dragon stepped aside.

It was a small movement for a body so large. His injured leg shook as he held his weight to one side, keeping a narrow passage open beside the wall. The man saw it. He hesitated, looking towards the dragon's head, then moved through with his shoulder pressed against the stone.
Ember did not follow.
He watched the green cloak disappear into the smoke, then turned away from the ruined stand.
A voice called from farther along the square.
Behind a wooden barrier stood a figure in a dark robe. The person was making the same sharp command again and again, one arm raised. Smoke kept hiding the face.
Ember moved towards the sound. His claws crushed pieces of fallen roof. Heat gathered in him once more, quick and terrible, and the dark figure drew back behind the wood.
The fire reached the barrier before he did.
Flame ran up its dry supports. Ember recoiled from the sudden crash as the structure folded into the space beyond it. He roared, but could no longer see the person who had called.
Other voices answered from the smoke.
None was Elara's.
He turned in the centre of the square, trying to separate them. The market was no longer a place he recognised. The hook, the awning, the counter: all were gone behind heat and falling ash.
He could stay. There were still voices to follow, still movements in the lanes.
Instead he looked towards the valley.
The stone was there.

He pushed off from the ruined ground. Smoke closed beneath his wings and broke apart as he rose. For a moment he could see the young man at the edge of the houses, one hand against a wall, looking up.
Ember passed over him.
Beyond the last roof, the air was cold enough to hurt his throat.

chapters.title: Beside the Stone
paragraphs: The mound had not changed.
Ember landed below it and climbed the last few steps with his wings partly spread for balance. His wounded foot left a dark mark on a stone. He stopped beside the grave and lowered his head.
The village smell was on him now.
Smoke clung to the folds of his wings. Ash had settled between his scales. When he breathed, he tasted the fire he had carried through the streets.
He pressed his nose to the broad stone.
It was cool.

He stayed there until his breathing slowed, then moved around the mound, examining the edges. A little soil had slipped where the ground fell away. He pushed it back. A blade of grass had bent across the place where her head lay. He left it.
Behind him, smoke rose above the roofs.
He did not look at it for long.
He had gone towards the hands that hurt her. They had opened, dropped what they held, disappeared into the houses. He had followed until the houses burned.

Now there was dirt across the bridge of his nose where he had touched the mound. He rubbed it against the stone, clearing the scent of smoke enough to find hers underneath. She remained where he had left her.

He lowered himself carefully beside the mound, keeping his weight away from its loose edge. One wing curved over the place where her body lay. It made a little shelter against the wind, although no part of her was exposed now.
The effort brought a tremor into the thin membrane.
He held it there.

From the village came the distant fall of timber. He raised his head, then settled again when he heard no footsteps approaching. The crow returned to the broken fence. This time it stayed on the farther post and made no attempt to come closer.
Ember closed his eyes.
He was small enough to fit beneath the table.

Elara's feet were moving beyond its legs. He could see the hem of her dress and the end of the cloth she carried. Each time it swung near, he reached for it. She moved it out of the way, laughing, and he shuffled forward to try again.
At last she crouched.

There was a little piece of meat in her fingers. He reached too quickly, and she drew it back. Wait. He knew the pause before the gift. He held still, though every part of him wanted to move, until she brought it to his mouth.
Afterwards her hand rested between his eyes.
He opened them.
The stone filled his sight.
He rested his forehead against the rough stone. There was no warmth in it yet. He breathed across it and waited.
Clouds moved over the slope. The light weakened, not suddenly but by small degrees. The hollow under his wing became darker. He shifted closer to the grave and drew his tail around his feet.
He had waited through her absences before.

There had been the smell of an empty room, the scrape of his claws against the floor, a sound outside that made him lift his head too early. Then the latch, the door, the familiar weight of her footsteps.
Sometimes she had spoken to him before she left.
He remembered the voice more clearly than the words. The way it softened at the end. The way she turned back once from the doorway because he was still watching her.
He listened for it now.
The wind came through the broken rails. Somewhere below, people were calling to one another. Nearer at hand, a small stone loosened from the bank and rolled into the grass.
Ember lifted his head at each sound.
Once, he rose halfway to his feet.
Then he lay down again.
The last light caught the pale edges of his horns. He tucked the wounded leg beneath his chest and kept his head close to the marker, leaving no space between stone and scales.
His mouth opened as he slept. Then it closed gently, as though her fingers had brought food to it and he was trying not to hurt them.
Night came slowly over the valley.
Beneath his breath, the stone began to warm.

chapters.title: Under the Earth
paragraphs: The warmth beneath his jaw did not fade when he stopped breathing on the stone.
Ember lifted his head. Snow had settled along the upper edge of his folded wing. He shook it loose, then lowered his nose to the mound beside the marker.
Earth. Wet wool. Her.
He knew those smells. What drew him closer was something inside his own chest: a faint tightening, followed by a release. It came again when he pressed his muzzle against the soil.
He had felt it before, asleep against her body when he was small enough for her arms. The movement had belonged to her then. Now it was beneath his scales, answering something he could not hear.
He moved his sound forefoot across the mound.
A little soil slid away. He stopped, remembering the care with which he had covered her, the cloth he had tucked close beneath her chin. The cold would reach her if he disturbed it.
The tightening came once more.
He dug.

Not with the force he had used to break the ground before. His claws drew shallow furrows through the loose earth, pushing it downhill. When they caught wool, he lifted his foot away. His muzzle did the rest, sweeping soil from a shoulder, then the hollow where her neck met the shawl.
Her face emerged slowly.
He breathed over it. Dust moved across her cheek. Nothing else changed.
The heat in him gathered behind his breastbone.

Ember recoiled. He knew what could follow that feeling. He turned his head away from her and opened his mouth, but no flame came. The heat remained inside him, held in a place he had never needed to notice before.
He looked back at the exposed face.
His mother had lain still when he brought her here. She had lain still while he covered her. He had pressed his nose against her hand until the fingers were cold, and she had not moved them once.
He touched her now with the unscaled edge of his lower jaw.
Something pulled.
He could have lifted his head. He almost did. His shoulders tensed, ready to break the contact, but her hair was against his mouth and he knew the smell beneath the earth.
He stayed.
Light appeared between the scales of his throat, pale enough to show their separate edges. It travelled down towards his chest, then rose again. He exhaled a thin, colourless breath across her skin.
The grass beside her did not burn.

The pulling deepened. His sound leg slid in the loose earth, and he drove his claws into the bank to hold himself still. There had been other kinds of pain: the rope, the first hard landing, the raw place he could not stop licking. This had no place he could reach with his tongue or draw away from the ground. It spread each time the light moved towards her.

He folded a wing over the side of the hollow to keep the wind from her face. The effort nearly broke the contact beneath his jaw. He lowered himself farther, ignoring the hurt leg, until his weight was settled against the earth and he no longer had to hold himself above her.
Her hand jerked.
Ember made a sound that startled birds from the ruined fence. He pushed closer, too quickly, and the light wavered. The pain sharpened. His hind feet scraped for a better hold on the slope.

He remembered being caught in cloth. Her fingers had freed his claw one joint at a time. He remembered waiting for food while she cut it small enough for him. He remembered the weight of her forehead against his.
He did not understand these things as a bargain.
He only knew what it was to stay.
The brightness left his throat. For a moment it hung against her chest beneath the torn dress, showing a branching shape through the fabric.
Then Elara drew breath.
There was dirt in her mouth.

She tried to spit and could not lift her head. Something heavy lay across her legs. Panic struck before she knew what she was afraid of. She fought the weight, caught a mouthful of cold air and coughed until her ribs seemed to separate.
A pale shape moved above her.
She threw up an arm.
It met scales.
“Ember?”

Her own voice frightened her. It came out torn and dry, hardly a voice at all. The shape lowered itself. His nose pressed into her hair with such urgency that she had to turn her face aside to breathe.
“Wait. Let me.”
He drew back at once.
She could see the stars through the ridges of his horns. Between her face and the sky lay a cut edge of earth, dark roots hanging from it.
A hole.
She was lying in a hole.

Elara sat up too suddenly. The world narrowed to a point of light, then returned with a surge of nausea. Loose earth fell from her dress. Her legs were covered to the knees. Beside her head stood a broad stone she did not recognise.
The last thing she remembered was a raised arm in the lane.
Not this slope. Not the night.

She tried to put the intervening time somewhere. A room where she had lain unconscious. A person who had carried her. Something she might remember if she could stop the shaking in her hands. But there was only the arm, the mud at her cheek, and then the taste of soil.

She heard someone breathing and turned towards them before she understood that it was herself. The sound was too loud inside her head. She pressed a palm against her mouth, frightened it might stop if she listened too closely.
Ember nosed at her wrist. She uncovered her mouth and drew another breath because he was watching.

She put her fingers to her cheek. Dried blood broke beneath them, but the skin underneath had closed. Her shoulder ached deeply when she moved it. Her hands were grazed and raw, just as they had been when she pulled the rope.
Ember watched her hands. His whole body trembled.
She stopped examining herself.
“Oh, love.”

He lowered his head until his brow rested against her knees. She held him there, one hand spread between the familiar ridges, the other gripping her own sleeve because she could not stop shaking either.
When she tried to stand, he offered his neck. She leaned against the solid curve and freed one foot, then the other. He rose only as fast as she did. Earth slid into the spaces her legs had left.
She looked down.
The hollow was shaped for her body. Her shawl lay in it, one end still caught beneath a clod. She pulled it free and wrapped it around herself, unable to look at the stone again.

Along the upper bank lay roots, pebbles, pieces of broken turf pushed carefully aside. His claw marks crossed and recrossed the soil. He had worked here. He had been alone here, doing something she could scarcely bear to imagine.
She wanted to ask why he had covered her. Then she saw him watching the shawl settle around her shoulders and understood how cruel the question would be, even if he could answer it.
“You stayed with me.”

His nose touched the cloth. She laid her cheek against the side of his face and did not ask him for anything else. There would be a time to be frightened of the hole. For now he needed to feel her move when he touched her.
Below them, a dull red glow marked the village.
Ember turned towards it. For an instant she saw the blackened scales along his muzzle and the ash lodged in the folds of his wings.
She knew him well enough to be afraid of what she did not remember.
Then his foreleg buckled.
Elara reached for him uselessly. His weight struck the ground with a force that shook her feet. He caught himself on his other leg and lay down, his breath coming in shallow bursts.
“What's wrong?”
He pressed his face into her hand.
The skin beneath his jaw was cold.

chapters.title: The Cold Breath
paragraphs: She had never felt him cold before.

Even in the cave, when she first lifted him, the little body had warmed her through wet cloth. Later, when she had sold the green cloak and could not feel her fingers, he had breathed over them until they hurt with returning life.
Now she held those same hands beneath his mouth and felt nothing warmer than the night.
Elara rubbed the folds of his throat. “Slowly. Don't try to stand yet.”
He seemed to think she wanted a fire.
His neck extended. The muscles beneath her palms tightened. He drew air through his nostrils, opened his jaws and strained.
A dry cough shook him.
Pain answered beneath her own ribs. She doubled over, one hand still on him, and waited for it to pass. When she could straighten, he was watching her with his mouth half open.
“Enough.”
He opened his mouth again, still trying to give her what he thought she needed. Elara moved round to face him. She held up her palm as she had when the jug was full and he came too close.
“Wait.”

The muscles in his neck remained taut. She lowered her shoulders deliberately, let her own breath out, and waited with him. At last his jaw loosened. He put his face into her palm, spent with the effort of doing nothing.
The effort had left his nostrils grey around the edges. A small pulse beat beneath the scales of his neck, too fast, then too slowly.
Something moved in her chest at the same uneven pace.
Elara loosened the shawl. A branching line lay beneath her collarbone, the colour of an old bruise. When his pulse faltered, a dull point of light travelled along it.
She pulled the cloth closed.

She had questions that would not fit inside her head. How long had she lain under the earth? Who had brought her here? What had happened to the village? But Ember's wounded foot was curled beneath him, and he could not keep his eyes open.
He needed help from someone who knew more than she did.
Nessa.
The name brought back a face beyond the stones. Eyes lowered. A hand that had stayed by its owner's side.
Elara looked towards the burning roofs and tried to think of anyone else.
The wind shifted. She smelt smoke, wet ash and the sharp scent of timber not yet consumed. Somewhere below, a voice called another person's name again and again.
“Can you walk?” she asked.
He lifted his head. The trust in that movement nearly undid her.
“Only a little way at first.”
She stood beside his sound foreleg, where he could see her without turning. He got up in stages. The wounded foot touched the ground last, claws spread to take less weight.
They went along the fence rather than down into the village. Every few steps Elara stopped. Sometimes it was for him. Sometimes she pretended it was for him because her own legs had begun to shake.
At the crest she looked back once.

The broken earth shone pale beside the dark stone. He had dug her out. She understood that much. She also understood, with a certainty she could not explain, that something which had lived inside him was now keeping her upright.
She could not yet bear to give that thought words.

At the next break in the fence she tried to step ahead and choose a path. Ember turned so quickly that the band of injured scales along his leg reopened. She heard the small cry and came back, angry with herself.
“I'm only looking.”
He remained upright until she put a hand on him. When she moved it away, he lifted his head.

She began again, more slowly. One step while keeping her fingers on his cheek. Another, within sight. She waited for his breathing to settle before going farther. It was what she had done with the door when he was small, except that now both of them flinched at the space between her hand and his face.
The minutes it took frightened her. So did the thought of hurrying him until he fell. She chose the wider route round the fence, where he would not have to watch her disappear behind a post.

Nessa's house stood beyond the old mill, where the stream curved away from the last gardens. Elara had been there once for a poultice when a winter cough would not leave her. She remembered herbs hanging from the beams and a door that opened towards the water.
Getting there meant crossing the cart track beneath the village.
She took Ember through the bare orchard. Branches scratched her face. He folded his wings close and followed the gaps she found, too tired to object when a dead limb caught against his shoulder.
At the track they stopped.

A cart stood tipped beside a ditch. Someone had piled blankets beneath it. Two children slept there, their faces striped with soot, while a woman knelt over a bucket farther away. Her hair was singed at the ends.
Elara recognised one of the blankets. It had hung outside the house opposite hers.
She looked at Ember.

He had turned his head from the smoke. Ash fell from his scales when he moved. There was no pride in his face, no triumph she could understand. He pressed against the nearest tree as though he wanted it between himself and the track.
“I know you were frightened,” she whispered.
She did not know what else to say. Those children had not thrown the stones. Neither had hers.

One of the children woke and pushed the blanket off her face. The woman came from the bucket, stooped beneath the cart and drew it back over her. Elara watched the hand remain there a moment, cupped round the small head.

She knew what it was to need the rest of the world to stay away while a child slept. That knowledge had not belonged to her alone. Beyond the orchard, other people had been doing it in rooms with doors and roofs. Now they were trying to do it under a broken cart.
“We can't do that again,” she whispered to Ember.

He turned at her voice. She could not tell him what the other mother feared, or make him see the market from somewhere outside his grief. She would have to learn how to keep him safe without letting that mean everyone else could burn. For now she laid her palm against the ash on his cheek and kept it there.
The woman straightened beside the cart and looked towards the orchard.
Elara stepped back into the orchard. She could not help them by being found here. She could barely remain standing herself.
They waited until the woman turned back to tend the children, then crossed behind her. Ember's claws sounded horribly loud on the frozen ruts. Elara counted each step without meaning to.
Nobody called out.
Beyond the mill, the stream covered the sound of their approach. One window in Nessa's house showed a faint orange light. Bundles had been dragged onto the doorstep. She was preparing to leave.
Elara knocked.
“Take the other path,” Nessa called from inside. “The bridge is blocked.”
“Open the door.”
A stool scraped. Footsteps stopped just beyond the wood.
Elara waited with one hand against Ember's cheek. His eyes were closed. She could feel him leaning more heavily towards her, though he kept most of his weight away by instinct.
The latch lifted.
Nessa held a lamp at shoulder height. The flame threw light across Elara's face, her blood-stiffened hair, the soil caught in the torn dress.
The old woman made no sound. Her wrist lowered until the lamp nearly touched the doorframe.
“He needs you,” Elara said.
Nessa looked beyond her at the vast pale shape standing in the dark. Then back at the face she had watched disappear beneath the crowd.
“I was there when they carried you away.”
“You were there before that.”
The words left no room for either of them to pretend.
Nessa steadied the lamp with her other hand. She took one step back, then changed direction and came outside.
“The lean-to,” she said. “He won't fit through this door.”
Elara did not thank her. She led her son towards the shelter and heard the old woman follow.

chapters.title: What Nessa Kept
paragraphs: The lean-to had been built for split wood and a small cart. Nessa dragged the cart into the yard. Ember lowered himself into the space it left, his hindquarters outside the roof, his injured foreleg stretched where the lamp could reach it.
Nessa approached from the side, showing him her empty hands.
“Does he understand you?”
“Enough.”
“Tell him I must touch the wound.”

Elara knelt beside his head. There were things she wanted to say to this woman that would have made it impossible to sit quietly beside her. She held them back while Nessa fetched warm water and strips of clean linen.

The rope had cut between the scales. Dirt and dried blood had formed a hard ridge along the groove. Nessa soaked it instead of pulling it free. Ember's claws scraped the earth once. Elara stroked the soft skin behind his jaw until they relaxed.
“It should have been cleaned sooner,” Nessa said.
“There was no one with him.”
The old woman bent closer to her work.

When the wound was clean, she dried it carefully. Her usual bandages were too narrow for his leg. She brought out a sheet, tore it lengthways and folded it into a broad strip, leaving room for his joints to move.
Elara watched those capable hands.
They had known what to do in a crisis all her life.
“Why didn't you come to me?” she asked.
Nessa did not pretend to misunderstand. “I was afraid.”
“Of him?”
“At first.”
“And when I was on the ground?”
The loose end of the bandage slipped from Nessa's fingers. She picked it up, smoothed the fold and tied the knot on the outside of the leg, away from the wound.
“Of what they would do if I went against them.”
“You went into my house with Marda.”
“I thought I could keep her from bringing others.”
Elara looked at the lamp. The flame moved each time wind came round the side of the shelter. She remembered another small light, the roof open above it, Nessa standing between the table and the wall.
“Did you catch the stool on purpose?”
“Yes.”
“Then you knew how to stop someone. You knew I needed you to.”
Nessa held the end of the linen in both hands. “I thought I had done enough that night.”
“You did enough to go home.”

Elara had not meant to raise her voice. Ember's head lifted at once, and the motion sent a tremor through his foreleg. She bent towards him until he rested again. When she next spoke to Nessa, it was quietly. That made the words no easier.
“I don't need you to tell me how afraid you were. I need you to remember what you chose while you were afraid.”

Elara looked beyond her at the sacks on the doorstep. A person could prepare to leave. A person could decide what to carry, open a door and go through it. She remembered how none of those choices had remained for her in the lane.
“You had time to be afraid.”
“Yes.”
It was not an apology. Perhaps an apology would have angered her more.
Ember shivered. Elara pulled her shawl from her shoulders and laid it beneath his jaw, then held it there when his breath began to come too quickly.
Nessa's gaze changed.
“Your neck.”
Elara looked down. The branching mark had darkened above the edge of her dress. A thin grey line extended towards her left shoulder.
Nessa reached out, then stopped before touching her.
“May I?”
“What is it?”
“Something I hoped never to see again.”

Elara let her move the torn collar aside. The mark divided over her breastbone, neither a wound nor a pattern drawn on the skin. When Nessa held her wrist and laid two fingers against the dragon's throat, the lines briefly brightened.
The old woman counted without speaking. She counted again, then released them both.
“Your mother carried a smaller mark after you were born.”
Elara stared at her.
“I helped bring you into the world. There was nothing unusual about you that anyone could see. A hungry baby. A mother who could not bear to put her down.”
“Why would she have this?”
“I need to show you something.”
“No. You need to tell me.”
Nessa accepted that too. She sat back on her heels, keeping her hands where Ember could see them.

“Long before either of us was born, there were nests in the northern mountains. Not one creature hidden in a woman's house. Whole families. Traders found that bone could be carved, blood could be sold, and fire could be taken from a living body if you hurt it for long enough.”
Elara's hand closed on the shawl.
“People who had never seen a dragon wanted a piece of one. The hunters followed the demand. They emptied the nests.”
“What has that to do with my mother?”

“Some families sheltered what remained. The dragons entrusted a spark to them. Not an egg they could seize, or a creature they could follow home. Something carried in the blood, through ordinary lives, sometimes for generations.”
Elara looked at her son. His eyes were open now, following a moth that had reached the lamp. He lifted his muzzle a little, then let it fall back onto the cloth.
“And you think that was in me.”
“I think your mother knew it might be.”
“Did she know what would happen?”
“Not this. She didn't speak of it as something certain.”

Elara stared at the little moth turning around the lamp. It kept moving into the heat and drawing back. She wanted a memory of her mother in which all this knowledge could have fitted. A look she had mistaken, something left unsaid. She could find none that proved anything. Nessa's story was making familiar things feel as though they had belonged to someone else.
“And I was meant to find out alone?”
“You weren't. That was my failure.”

The distinction mattered. Elara did not want her mother's silence turned into permission for everything Nessa had done since. She would have questions for the woman who had given birth to her and was not here to answer them. The woman in front of her could answer for herself.

Nessa went inside and returned with a narrow book wrapped in oilskin. Its leather had worn away along the spine. Between two pages lay a drawing of a human torso, a branching mark inked beneath the collarbones. Beside it was the outline of a dragon curled around an egg.
The mark was not precisely like Elara's. It divided in the same places.
“She asked me to keep this,” Nessa said. “She wanted you to live without being watched for a sign. If the mark appeared in you, I was to tell you.”
“You asked about my ribs.”
The morning at her door returned with painful clarity. A leather bag. A question she had scarcely heard.
“I did.”
“In my house, when Marda was searching. What did you actually see?”
“I saw part of a wing.”
Elara got up. Too quickly. She caught the roof post to stop the yard from tipping beneath her.
Nessa began to rise after her.
“Stay there.”
The old woman stayed.
“You let me think I was alone in this.”
“I told myself you would come when you were ready.”
“I was buying meat with everything I owned.”
“I know.”
“You bought my cloak.”
Nessa closed the book. Her thumb remained between the pages, holding the place.
“There isn't an explanation that will make what I did kind,” she said.
For a moment Elara wanted to take the lamp and leave. She wanted her son away from these hands, this house, the whole village that had watched them suffer.
Then Ember tried to get up because she was standing.
His bandaged leg shook. She knelt before he could put his weight on it and guided his head down again.
“Rest. I'm still here.”
She looked at Nessa across his neck.
“Whatever you kept from me, you tell me now. You don't decide again what I can bear.”
“I won't.”
“And if you don't know something, say that. Don't make it sound certain to keep me quiet.”

Nessa nodded. She put the bag beside Elara instead of keeping it behind her own knees, where its contents were hidden. Clean linen, the little knife for cutting it, the covered ointment pot. Practical things Elara could see and take. It was a small surrender of authority, and she accepted it without mistaking it for forgiveness.
Nessa opened the book and moved the lamp closer.

chapters.title: Before the Second Sunset
paragraphs: The book did not contain a cure.

Elara understood that before Nessa said it. There were no measured doses beside the drawing, no list of things to boil. The notes were written in different hands, some careful, some cramped into the margins. A person had crossed out one whole passage so fiercely that the paper had torn.
“These are accounts,” Nessa said. “What people saw. What they tried.”
“And what happened to them?”
Nessa turned a page instead of answering immediately.
Elara made her turn it back.
Beneath the crossing-out was a date, then another two days later. Beside the second, someone had drawn two short vertical strokes. No names. Nothing after them.
Nessa rested a finger against the margin. “The mother woke. The child lost his heat. By the second evening, both were gone.”
Ember's breath lifted the shawl between them.
“How many?”
“There are three such accounts here. One describes a return from the first nest. That pair survived.”
It was so little knowledge to place against his life. Elara looked at the book, then at the woman who had kept it closed while she sold the things that might have carried them away.
“Tell me how I came back.”
Nessa held her wrist again, gently enough that she could pull away.
“When he grew inside you, part of your living warmth became his. More than it would with a human child. It remained bound to you after he was born.”
“So there was something inside my baby. Something that changed him.”
“Not another creature. There wasn't a different son taken from you and replaced. The spark grew as he grew. This is the child you carried.”
Elara looked at the familiar line of his jaw. She had once been frightened to touch it. Later she had searched it for splinters after he broke the roof.
She put her hand there now.
“And at the grave?”
“Your body had stopped. But the part of your life he carried had not. He found a way to send it back.”
Elara remembered a pressure in the dark, then earth in her mouth. She could not reach anything before that. There was no hidden interval in which she had waited knowingly to be rescued.
“He brought more than you needed,” Nessa continued. “He kept nothing safely apart. The warmth is passing between you now without settling in either body.”
As she spoke, Ember stirred. Heat prickled along Elara's mark, then vanished, leaving her colder than before.
“Can he take it back?”
“Not by himself.”
“If I die again?”
Nessa's hand tightened. “That would not undo this. It would break what still joins you. He cannot bring you back a second time.”
Elara let the question end there. She was glad, fiercely and ashamedly glad, that her death was not a useful thing to offer.
“Where is the nest?”

Nessa unfolded a page larger than the rest. The route on it followed water, not roads. A split ridge, a stone bridge, the mouth of a spring beneath a leaning slab. Elara knew the stream at the bottom. She had never gone beyond the bridge.
“North of the quarry. Behind the fall where the water comes out of the mountain.”
“How will he get through a waterfall? He can barely stand.”
“There is an opening at its eastern edge. It was sealed from the valley path. The record gives another way in.”
Beside the route was a drawing of a broad, shallow basin carved into the floor. Lines ran out from it towards smaller hollows. A darker stone lay at its centre.
“The heart-stone belonged to the nesting ground. It held the warmth between a mother and her eggs. The surviving account says it steadied the bond between a woman and her child.”
“How?”
“They reached it together. Both remained in contact with it while the current settled.”
“That's all?”
“That's all that is written.”

Elara leaned closer to the drawing. One edge of the basin had been redrawn, the second curve wider than the first. Someone had tried to correct the size. It was the sort of mistake she might make in a pattern for a garment, seeing a shape in her mind and then discovering there had to be room for a real body inside it.
“You've never been there.”
“No.”
“Or seen this happen.”
“No.”
Elara shut her eyes, then opened them. “Then show me which parts you are guessing.”

Nessa drew the book between them. She separated the oldest writing from the later notes, pointing out where a different hand had repeated a claim rather than witnessed it. She could recognise the sign for a nesting place. She could not promise that the entrance was still open, or that warmth which had settled once would settle again in exactly the same way.
“Why should a stone do what we can't?”
“It was made to hold warmth without taking it for a life of its own. Neither of you can do that now. You keep trying to keep each other alive, and neither can rest.”
“So we aren't looking for something to make him stronger.”
“First you need him to stop giving everything away.”

Elara put her hand near his eye. He followed it, too tired to move his head. She thought of the way he had strained for a flame on the hillside because her hands were cold. Even now she had been asking him to walk, to listen, to keep trying. It frightened her to wonder whether he knew she wanted him to live for any reason beyond what he could do for her.
Nessa did not dress her ignorance as wisdom. Elara would not have forgiven her if she had.
Outside, the sky had begun to lighten. They had used part of the night already.
“The second sunset from when he woke me,” Elara said.
“You must get there before then. Sooner if you can. I cannot promise that your bodies will last as long as the others did.”
“And if we find it and nothing happens?”
Nessa looked at the book. There was no page she could turn to answer that.
“I can treat his leg. I can give you food and somewhere out of the wind. I don't have another way to steady what joins you.”

Elara wanted to stay beside the lamp until someone arrived with a better answer. Instead she pulled the paper closer. She had taken a child down a mountain without knowing how to hold him. Knowing less than she needed had never stopped the next thing from being necessary.
“Copy the route,” she said. “Big enough to read in poor light.”
Elara studied the route until she could see it with her eyes closed. Nessa copied the essential turns onto a separate sheet. The original book was too fragile to take into the wet.
They packed bread, dried meat, linen, a tinderbox and a covered pot of ointment. Nessa put the paper inside a piece of oilskin and tied it with cord.

Elara counted the food. She separated the tinder from the meat, checked the lid of the ointment pot and asked for a small knife. Nessa gave her the one she had used on the bandages. Its handle was smooth from years of work. Elara wrapped the blade in a strip of linen before putting it inside the bundle; she could not afford to reach for food and cut the hands he needed.
Then Nessa brought out a green cloak.
Elara recognised the stitches at once.
“Take it,” Nessa said.
She did. Pride would not keep either of them warm.
Nessa watched her fasten it. “I can come as far as the bridge.”
A knock sounded at the front door. A man's voice asked for bandages. His wife's hand was burned; he did not know what to do.
Elara looked at the old woman.
“Help her.”
“The stream will be difficult with his leg.”
“You have told me the way. She is asking you to open the door.”
Nessa stood very still. Then she gathered her bag.

Elara led Ember out behind the lean-to, away from the waiting man. Before they reached the trees, she glanced back. Nessa was kneeling beside the injured woman, unwrapping the hand in full view of the lane.
It did not change what had happened.
It was something she should have done before.
Marda found Father Eldon beside the chapel wall.
One sleeve had burned away from his wrist. A strip of linen covered the skin beneath. He had survived the night behind stone while the sheds below the chapel collapsed.
She told him what she had seen near the mill: the pale back moving between trees, a woman in the torn dress of someone who had been carried from the village without breath.
He made her repeat it.
Then they went to the grave.
The earth lay open. Tracks led away from it, one set of claws dragging more deeply than the rest. Beside them were the marks of human feet.
Eldon stared until Marda asked what they should do.
He could have called the return a mercy. He could have let the valley keep the two lives he had tried to drive from it.
Instead he looked north, where the tracks continued towards the mill.
Marda was waiting for him to name what they had found. She had brought him fear once and received a promise to look. Now the open grave lay between them, offering an answer neither had asked for.
“If people see her,” Marda said, “what will you tell them?”
Eldon adjusted the linen around his burned wrist. Beyond the fence, women were carrying what could be saved from the houses. He watched them for a moment. Then he turned away from the village.
“Find the men who can still walk,” he said.

chapters.title: The Way Beyond the Bridge
paragraphs: By midday, the bandage was wet through.

Elara had stopped trying to keep count of their rests. She chose places out of the wind and let Ember decide when to get up. If she moved too soon, he followed her, even when his injured foot scarcely touched the ground.
She could not make him understand that being left for a moment was different from being left beneath the earth.
Sometimes she was not certain she understood it herself.

At a bend in the stream, she found a flat stone and put the food on it. Ember smelt the dried meat. Usually he would have taken it before she had finished arranging the pieces. Now he turned his head away.
She took a bite of bread to show him, chewing slowly around the soreness in her mouth. He watched. She offered meat again.
He swallowed one piece and closed his eyes.
Elara wrapped the rest. “We'll save it.”
Her voice sounded brisk and foolish in the empty valley. She was speaking as though they had a long ordinary day ahead, as though she might scold him for stealing supper later.
She let the pretence last while she changed the bandage.
The wound itself looked cleaner. It was everything around it that frightened her: the dull scales, the tremor that continued even when his leg was still. Ointment could not mend that.
She laid a clean folded strip over the groove and tied it as Nessa had shown her.
“Ready?”
His eyes opened before she had finished the word.

She did not rise immediately. Instead she held the folded paper where the light fell on it and waited until he had stretched his sound foreleg. He put the other foot down gingerly, tested it, then pushed himself upright. By not moving first, she had let him choose the moment.

It took longer than she wanted. She watched a strip of sunlight crawl across the opposite bank and tried not to count the time. When he was standing securely, he touched his nose to her shoulder. Then she put away the paper and walked.
The bridge had lost half its deck.

Elara stood on the bank and looked at the boards caught between the supports below. Meltwater had forced them loose. The remaining planks might have held a person, but the gap between the stone parapets was too narrow for Ember's chest.
On the copied map, the route continued on the opposite bank.
She looked upstream. The gorge narrowed there, which made the water faster. Downstream it spread into a shallower channel broken by pale gravel bars.
Ember extended his wings.
“Not over it.”

He kept them raised a moment, uncertain. She thought of his first flight, the terrible hope of seeing him clear the roofs. Now the muscles along his shoulders shook beneath the weight of the membranes.
He folded them again.

They followed the bank to the gravel. Elara found a long branch and tested the nearest water. It reached above her knee, then dropped sharply a pace farther out. She withdrew before the current could turn her sideways.
There would be no carrying him. No pulling him by a rope as if she were stronger than he was. She had to find a way he could cross under his own weight.
Farther down, a fallen tree divided the stream. Gravel had collected above it, making a sloping shelf. The water broke white around the exposed branches but ran more gently across the shelf itself.
