She walked the edge with the stick. One step. Test the depth. Another. Beyond the first stretch was a bar wide enough for all four of his feet.
She returned and pressed her hand to the sound side of his neck.

Before entering the stream, she fastened the bundle higher across her back. She tucked the front of her skirt into her belt and loosened the fastening at her throat; if the cloak caught in a branch, she wanted to be able to let it go. It was the only warm garment she had, but she had begun to understand what would happen if she treated anything they carried as more precious than getting through.
“Here. Watch where I put my feet.”
He followed her into the water.

Cold struck through her boots. The current tugged her skirt against her knees. She kept the stick downstream and moved sideways, leaving him room beside her rather than letting him walk directly behind.
For a few steps, it worked.
Then his wounded foot slipped on a rounded stone.
His shoulder lurched towards her. Elara stepped back to avoid being crushed and found nothing beneath her heel. Water took her to the waist. She lost the stick.
Ember turned his head so sharply that one horn passed inches from her face.
She caught the thick ridge at the base of his neck with both hands.
Pain tore through her shoulder. She held on. Her boots struck stones without finding purchase, and for a moment she felt him being drawn sideways too.
“Forward,” she gasped. “Keep going.”

His sound forefoot reached the gravel bar. He drove his claws into it, lowered his body and pushed with both hind legs. She dragged herself along the outside of his neck until one knee struck the shelf.
They came out together, heaving water onto the stones.
Elara lay on her side with her hands still clenched. Ember put his nose beneath her elbow and tried to lift her.
“I'm up. I'm getting up.”
She made herself do it before he could hurt his leg again. Her shoulder burned. Water poured from the hem of the cloak she had regained only hours before.

The far bank was nearer now. She sat with him until her breathing slowed, then tested the last shallow stretch with a shorter branch. She crossed just behind his sound shoulder, on the downstream side, where his body softened the current.
When they reached dry ground, she laughed once, a hard, breathless sound. He looked at her, startled.
She put her forehead against his wet scales.
“I know. That was a stupid place to fall.”
His nostrils moved against her hair. For a moment, beneath the fear and fatigue, there was the old child who had sneezed at a splinter from the roof.
She held on to that moment as they climbed.

The slope above the ford was broken by shelves of grass. Elara chose the nearest and began to climb towards it, then heard the scrape of Ember stopping behind her. His claws could not grip the thin wet turf. He tried once, slipped backwards, and looked at her.
She had nearly called him again before she understood. A place her feet could reach was not necessarily a place that would hold his weight.
“All right. Show me.”

She came down and waited. He moved along the bank, nosing at the stones until he found a slope where the rock lay exposed. He climbed with his body low and his wings partly open. The way was farther from the path on the paper, but at the top they reached the same strip of higher ground.
Elara followed, one hand pressed against her aching shoulder. He stopped above her instead of coming back down. She looked up at him and lifted her empty hand.
“That was better.”
He lowered his face when she reached him. She stroked it, then let him go ahead to the next turn. For a little while she did not have to know everything first.
The first sunset found them in the abandoned quarry.

They had followed the broad hauling track into the cut, where high rock sheltered them from the wind. The road ahead rose steeply beyond it. Elara could see the notch marked on Nessa's map, dark against the last of the sky.
She could not make herself walk towards it.
Her wet clothes had begun to stiffen. Ember lay beneath an overhang, unable to lift his head for long. The branching mark on her chest had reached her shoulder, and the skin along it felt numb.
She built a small fire in the lee of a fallen block, using dry splinters from an old wooden wedge. Nessa's tinder had stayed dry inside the oilskin. It took three attempts before a flame caught.
Ember opened his eyes at the sound.
He watched her feed it. When the light steadied, he looked from the fire to her hands.
“I can do this part,” she told him.
She dried the cloak first, turning it carefully so it did not scorch, then spread it over the lower curve of his neck. Her own skirt steamed as she sat close to the flames.
The fire might show through the quarry mouth. She knew that. They would not reach anything if they froze here.
From below came a sound that was not water.
She rose and stepped behind the block. Far below, on the opposite bank of the stream, a point of light disappeared behind trees. Then a second followed it.
People walking with covered lamps.
They were too far away for her to hear voices. They had come from the village, but the lights stopped at the broken bridge. While she watched, none crossed the water.

Elara returned to the fire and banked it low. She made a bed for herself against Ember's shoulder, where she could feel each breath, and drew the free end of the cloak across her legs. The food lay between them. After a while he took another small piece.
She listened for footsteps until she could no longer keep her eyes open.

Whenever she began to drift off, the blanket of her own cloak felt like soil settling over her legs. She dragged one foot free, breathed, and put it back beneath the cloth because the cold was worse. Ember watched each movement. He lifted his head when her breath caught, ready to get up although there was nowhere to go.
She sat upright and put her back against the rock.
“I'm afraid,” she told him.

It was a relief not to disguise it as something he needed to do differently. She showed him her hand and let him choose whether to bring his face close. When he did, she rested her fingers lightly against the scales.
“I don't know how to stop being afraid of that hole. You don't have to fix it.”

He breathed out, cool against her wrist. She counted the breaths without trying to make them deeper. At last his head settled on the edge of the cloak. He was still awake, but he was no longer preparing to rise every time she moved.

She took another bite of bread. There was grit in it from the wrapping, and she picked the grit out with a fingernail. A small, fussy task. Something she could finish. She gave him the last scrap of meat from the open portion, wrapped the rest and made herself swallow.

When she lay down again, she left her face and one hand outside the cloak. The rock at her back was solid. She could hear water below the quarry. She knew where she was, and her son was breathing beside her.
Before sleep took her, she looked up at the notch in the ridge.
One sunset remained.

chapters.title: The First Nest
paragraphs: The fire was cold when Elara woke.
For a moment she could not feel Ember breathing. She pushed herself upright, saying his name too loudly, and he shifted beneath her hand.
Relief made her angry. At the cold. At the distance still ahead. At herself for sleeping when she should have watched him.
She bit down on all of it. He needed her hands steady.
They left before the quarry filled with daylight.
Across the stream, five men were packing away the lamps they had not dared use to find a crossing in the dark.

The father of the two girls stood with his hands tucked beneath his arms. He had spent the night thinking of the place under the cart where the younger one was sleeping. He said they should go back and fetch others if they meant to confront something that had burned the market.
Eldon pointed at the marks in the opposite bank. Even from here they could see the churned earth where a heavy body had struggled out of the water.
“It is failing.”
“Then perhaps it will go somewhere else.”

The priest looked at him until he looked down. There were four men besides Eldon, and none wished to be the first to say he would leave. They followed the bank below the broken bridge until they found the gravel shelf. The man carrying rope went first, testing his footing, while another held the loose end from the bank.
Above them, Elara had already disappeared beyond the quarry wall.

Ahead of Elara, the hauling track became a ledge, then a slope of broken stones. She searched for the marks on Nessa's drawing: the divided ridge, the narrow bed of a dry stream, the fallen slab pointing towards the opposite face of the mountain.

At each turn, she stopped to compare the paper with the land. The drawing was old. One line that might once have marked a path now led to a fresh fall of rock. She had to go higher, crossing the slope until she found the dry streambed from the other side.

She folded back the portion they had travelled instead of trying to hold the whole sheet open in the wind. The bridge was behind them. The divided ridge was ahead. Between those two facts there were only a few marks, and she examined each one against the ground before asking Ember to follow.

At a narrow shelf she moved loose stones with her boots. He could not lift his wounded foot high enough to step over them safely. The work cost her more breath than she expected. When she paused to catch it, Ember pushed his muzzle against her back, trying to help her stand.
“Not that way. You'll send me over the edge.”
He withdrew. She made herself turn and touch him before starting again, so the last thing between them would not be her sharp voice.
Ember waited below while she checked the way. She made sure he could see her. Each time she returned, he touched her hand with his nose before taking another step.
As the sun rose, the light along her mark became visible through the collar of her dress. It did not warm her.
Twice she felt him stumble behind her and knew it in her chest before she turned.
They reached the leaning slab late in the afternoon.

Water sounded beyond it, louder than she expected. It came from a fissure in the mountain and spread over a smooth face of rock before falling into the valley. Spray had frozen along the edges, making thin curtains of ice.
Elara took out the paper.
The eastern edge. She checked the sun, then moved to her right along the base of the fall.
There was no opening.
She searched higher, keeping one hand on the wet stone. Moss covered a shelf just beyond reach. Below it was a narrow crack, scarcely wide enough for her arm, certainly not for her son.
“No.”
She went back to the slab and unfolded the paper completely. A corner she had kept beneath her thumb showed a short line running behind the fall, not beneath it.
She had approached too low.
Above them, on the far side of the slab, the dry streambed continued upwards. Its last few paces were hidden by the overhang. She had mistaken the end of the visible path for the end of the route.
Elara put the paper away and climbed.

The ledge widened behind the falling water. A dark passage opened at its end, broad enough for a cart and higher than Ember with his head lowered. Water had left a strip of smooth stone down the middle, but the sides were dry.
She bent double and cried once into her hands.
Then she went back for him.
Ember stopped at the entrance.
His head rose a little. He drew air slowly through his nostrils, tasting something beyond the damp stone. For the first time since the grave, he moved ahead of her.
She let him choose the pace.
The passage widened as it went deeper. Light came from a split in the roof, catching the mineral seams of the walls. Farther in, those seams held a pale glow of their own.
They emerged into a chamber so large that Elara could not see its far end.
The floor was divided into shallow hollows. Some were empty. Others held rounded shapes taller than her waist, their surfaces patterned with lines that resembled the branching mark beneath her skin.
Eggs.
She stopped beside the nearest one without touching it.

The shell was not smooth. Fine ridges crossed its surface, each one branching without quite repeating the next. At its base lay a curl of translucent material, something shed long ago and almost fused to the floor. Elara crouched to look. The hollows were not all the same size. Some had a broad worn place beside them where a much larger body might once have rested.

She placed her hand over that worn patch without pressing down. It was as wide as the hearth at home. She could imagine the daily movement that had made it: a head lowering, a parent settling, the same small space made comfortable over years. The scale was unfamiliar. The care was not.

There were more beyond it, half hidden behind pillars formed by water and time. Not heaps of treasure. Not carved stone. Individual shells, some pale, some almost black, each resting in its own hollow.
Ember breathed against one. A faint colour stirred beneath its surface.
Elara put a hand over her mouth.
She had spent so long believing there was no one else like him. She had studied his hunger, his wings, each new scale as though she might be the only person ever asked to understand such things.
Here were answers she did not have time to read.

She wanted to stay beside the nearest shell until it moved again. Instead she took out the paper and looked for the heart-stone. Having found a place where he belonged would mean nothing if she let him die at its entrance.

At the centre of the chamber lay the basin from Nessa's drawing. It was much wider than the page had made it seem, large enough for Ember to lie inside. Grooves led from its rim towards the nests. The heart-stone rose from the middle, dark and smooth, with a shallow curve worn into its upper surface.
Elara stepped over the rim.

She slipped the bundle from her shoulder and set it just inside the basin, clear of the grooves. Her fingers were stiff when she straightened them. She rubbed one hand against her skirt before reaching for the dark surface.
The stone was neither warm nor cold beneath her palm. At first she felt nothing. Then the mark along her chest tightened, pulling her attention down into her own body.
“Here,” she said. “Come beside me.”
Ember put one forefoot into the basin.
His knees gave way.
She moved clear as his weight struck the floor. His head came down short of the heart-stone, chin scraping across the shallow basin. He tried to lift it and could not.
Elara knelt beside him. The chamber seemed to tilt around her. Her palm left the stone, and the pulling sensation vanished.
They both had to touch it.
She cleared the bandaged leg from beneath his chest so he could breathe more easily. Then she folded her cloak beneath the lower curve of his jaw, making a pad where the stone's edge pressed into it.
“Just your head. You don't have to stand.”

He lifted it a fraction. She pushed the folded cloth forward, guiding rather than carrying his weight. His jaw slid beyond the cloth onto the low lip of the heart-stone. She left the cloak beneath his neck as a cushion, with the bare scales of his chin against the smooth surface.
A line of light appeared in the basin.
Elara placed both hands beside his face.

For a moment she heard two separate rhythms, one beneath her palms and one inside her chest. They stumbled against each other. The stone vibrated faintly, like a cup set on a table above moving machinery.
Outside the chamber, a foot scraped rock.
She looked towards the passage.
Father Eldon stood at its mouth with four men behind him. Their lamps were unnecessary here. One carried a length of rope. Another had brought a woodcutter's axe.
The man with the axe looked past Elara at the nearest egg.
“There are more.”
Eldon raised a hand to keep him still. His eyes moved over the chamber, measuring the rows of shells, the dragon on the floor, the woman whose death he had called a deliverance.
Elara kept one hand on the heart-stone.
“You have followed us far enough,” she said.

chapters.title: What They Would Not Take
paragraphs: Eldon entered the chamber slowly.
The men spread out behind him, keeping the passage within reach. They watched the eggs as if something might break through the shells at any moment.
Elara looked only at their hands.
Rope. Axe. A stout wooden staff. The fourth man's hands trembled as he set down his lamp.
She recognised him. Once, outside his door, she had seen his two little girls arguing over a ribbon.
“You can still leave,” she said.
“You burned our homes,” he answered.
She had not. Yet denying it seemed a coward's answer with Ember beside her and soot still caught beneath his scales.
“I saw the cart below the orchard. The children under it.”
The man swallowed. “One of them is mine.”
“Then go back to her.”
“With that thing alive?” Eldon said.
The father looked at the dragon's bandaged leg. His gaze remained there longer than Elara expected.
“Was it wounded before the fire?” he asked.
“The rope did that. Outside my house.”
“It doesn't give it leave to burn my children.”
“No.”
She had wanted someone to ask what had been done to them. Now that he had, she could not use the answer to make his loss smaller. His hand closed around the lamp handle. Neither of them looked away.
Eldon stepped between their lines of sight.
Ember's eyes opened at his voice. His jaw moved against the stone, and Elara felt the rhythm falter beneath her palm.
“Stay with me,” she murmured.
The priest heard her. His gaze settled on their hands and scales touching the dark surface. He took another step.
“It cannot protect you now.”
“I haven't asked it to.”
Her mouth had used his word. It. She hated that, hated the ease with which fear made her speak a language she did not accept.
“My son,” she said, more clearly. “His name is Ember.”
Behind Eldon, the axe shifted in its owner's grip. He was looking at the nearest shell.
“Leave that,” Elara said.
He stopped.
The axe head had risen scarcely above his knee, but Elara could see where he meant to put it. One blow into the shell nearest the passage, then another. He would not have to approach Ember at all.
“What if it opens?” the father asked him.

The man with the axe glanced at the rows of eggs beyond it. He lowered the blade an inch. Fear had kept him from acting where compassion might not have. Elara accepted the pause without trying to call it anything better.
The priest did not turn. “You see what she has brought us to. If these hatch, the valley will never belong to our children again.”
“Your children are down the mountain. They need roofs. Water. Someone to hold them after last night.”
“They need this ended.”
Eldon stepped across the basin's rim.

Elara rose into a crouch between him and Ember's face, keeping her left palm on the heart-stone. She could not cover the dragon with her body. She could only make the place where he was most vulnerable a little harder to reach.
The priest drew a short knife from his belt.

Nessa's knife was in Elara's bundle, where she had set it at the edge of the basin. She could reach it only by leaving the stone. Then she would have to find it beneath the food and unwrap the blade. Even if Eldon gave her time, she would have to use it with fingers that shook and an arm she could barely lift.
She moved her heel against the bundle and pushed it farther behind her. He would not get that knife as well.
She remembered an arm rising above the crowd. The way each person had waited for someone else to make the next act possible. Her shoulder began to shake, but she held out her free hand.
“You were wrong about him.”
“I watched the roofs burn.”
“And you watched me die before that. Don't speak as though this began with fire.”
His face tightened. Beneath his anger, she thought she recognised fear. She had returned to a world in which he had already explained her death.
He reached for her wrist.

Elara caught his sleeve instead and pushed it aside. Pain shot through her injured shoulder. Her knees struck the floor. She managed to keep her left hand where it was, but two fingers slid from the stone.
The glow in the grooves weakened.
Ember's head rose an inch. He tried to open his mouth.
“No,” she told him. “Not yet.”
The man with the staff stepped forward, then stopped when the dragon looked at him. Ember could scarcely hold up his head, but the man kept his distance.
Elara used that hesitation to place her right hand against her son's jaw and ease it back onto the stone.

For a few breaths, nobody came closer. The father had put one foot across the basin's rim, in the way of the man carrying the staff. He did not look towards Elara. He watched the knife, his own empty hand half raised as if he had not yet decided what to do with it.
The heart-stone vibrated beneath her palm. Heat flooded her chest, so suddenly that she gasped. Ember's eyes began to close.
It was happening again. Whatever moved between them was leaving him to keep her alive.
She pulled her body back without lifting her hand, as though distance alone could refuse the gift. The heat faltered. Pain followed it into her ribs.
“I need you here,” she whispered. “Not just what you can give me.”

Ember tried to lift his head towards her. She knew the effort now: she moved, and he followed; she was cold, and he strained for fire. Even with his life failing, he was looking for the thing she wanted him to do.

She let her right hand rest beside his jaw instead of using it to guide him. She stopped urging his face into place. The folded cloak already supported his neck, and the stone was beneath his chin. He did not need to hold himself up for her.
“Stay as you are.”

His gaze went to her open fingers. The muscles along his neck trembled, then loosened. Elara felt a fraction of the heat in her own chest settle lower, no longer rushing towards her throat. She resisted the urge to seize him when it happened. She had asked him to wait so often. Now she had to do it too.

Eldon shifted closer. Her fingers closed against the familiar edge of Ember's lower jaw before she could stop them. She had held him there when he wanted food too quickly, when he was frightened by a noise, when the room seemed too small to contain them both.
She took a slow breath.
His nostrils moved.
She waited for him before breathing again.

The two rhythms touched, slipped apart, then returned closer together. It was not a command the stone obeyed. She could feel how readily they might lose it, how his effort to comfort her pulled too much warmth in one direction, how her fear made her grip him harder when she should have stayed still.
She loosened her fingers.
Eldon seized the back of her dress.
The collar caught beneath her throat. She let her weight fall instead of rising with his pull. The cloth tore at a seam. Her hand remained against the stone.
“Help me,” he snapped at the men.
The father beside the lamp looked from the knife to Elara's face.
“Put that away first.”
“You saw what it did.”
“I see what you're doing.”
Eldon pulled again. Elara could not hold much longer. Her fingertips were slippery with sweat, her shoulder a bright point of pain.
Then warmth settled beneath her hand.
Not the terrible rush that had filled her chest. Something steady, held in the stone and in the living jaw beside it. Ember's next breath was warm enough to stir heat against her cheek.
The mark beneath her collar brightened from end to end.
She cried out. So did he.

Light ran through the grooves of the basin and into the hollows beyond it. The shells answered one after another, a slow kindling through their branching lines. The knife in Eldon's hand caught the light and flashed white.
He let go of the torn cloth.
Ember lifted his head.
This time he held it there.

Elara kept one hand on the stone as he unfolded his sound foreleg beneath his chest. The injured one followed more carefully. His eyes had cleared. He looked at the knife, then at the man who held it.
Heat gathered in his throat.
Elara moved beside his head, clear of the line between his jaws and Eldon. This time she did not ask him to flee.
“Only enough,” she said.
His flame struck the empty stone between the priest and the basin's rim.
It lasted less than a breath. Eldon stumbled backwards. The end of the rope, dropped by the man behind him, blackened and curled. Then Ember closed his mouth.
The fire was out.
The man with the axe lowered its head to the floor. The father picked up his lamp. Neither moved to help Eldon forward again.

Ember watched the rope. Elara saw his eyes follow its blackened end, the way his lip lifted before he hid the teeth again. His injured foot remained half raised. Nothing that had frightened him had vanished when his strength returned.

She kept her hand near his cheek without closing it against him. He could see the men move. She would not make him turn away and pretend they were harmless. But when the father took a slow step towards the passage, she left him room to do it. Ember's head followed. His mouth stayed closed.
Elara looked at them across the scorched stone.
“Go home to the people who are waiting for you.”
The father paused beside the basin.
“What do I tell them?”
“What you saw. That we were alive when you found us. That we let you leave.”

He looked towards Eldon, then back at the scorch on the floor. He gave one short nod. Elara could not know what he would say once the mountain lay between them. She had asked for the truth, not a promise to love her child.
The others said nothing. The man with the lamp turned towards the passage, and they followed him.
Eldon remained a moment longer. His knife was still in his hand. He looked towards the eggs as though searching for an argument that would bring the men back.
Behind Elara, Ember breathed quietly.
At last the priest stepped out of the basin.
She watched him until the passage hid him. Only then did she realise that her hand had left the heart-stone.
Her heart was still beating.

chapters.title: A Place to Stay
paragraphs: Elara waited until she could no longer hear their footsteps.
Then her legs gave way.
Ember lowered himself beside her, slowly enough not to crush the folds of her dress. She put both arms around as much of his neck as she could reach and held on.

She had words prepared. Sensible words about resting, eating, keeping the bandage dry. None of them came. She cried against his scales until her chest hurt, and he stayed so still that she might have been holding him rather than the other way around.
When she drew back, there was a wet patch beneath his jaw.
“Look at the state of us.”
He touched her shoulder with his nose. She flinched from the bruise, and he withdrew at once.

The pain was almost reassuring. It belonged to a part of her that was hurt and would need time. It did not travel into him. When he flexed his injured foot, she felt no answering pull beneath her ribs.
She checked his pulse, then her own. She could not count them accurately. Her fingers shook too much, and she had never learned what was ordinary for a dragon.
But neither seemed to be dragging the other towards silence.
She took her hand from him and waited. One breath, then several more. His chest continued to rise. Her own heart went on without the strange dragging beat that had frightened her on the hillside.
Ember watched the withdrawn hand. She showed him the empty palm, then used it to wipe her face. For once, he did not try to get up when she moved.
That was when she began to believe they had come through it. Not when the stone lit, or the fire made the men step back, but when she could reach for her own sleeve and he could rest.
The branching mark had faded to a pale scar.
Elara touched it through the torn collar. She would have that to explain if she ever chose to explain herself again. For now she let the cloth fall back into place.
Along the chamber floor, the light in the grooves softened. It remained in the nests, moving slowly beneath the shells.
Ember raised his head.
“What is it?”
He listened towards the nearest egg. A small sound came from within, too faint for her to recognise until she put her palm close to the surface without quite touching it.
A movement. A tiny scrape.
There was a child inside.

She drew her hand back instead of touching the shell. She knew almost nothing about the life moving beneath it. Whether it needed heat, quiet, another sound from Ember. Since the cave she had been trying to make room for one child inside the things she understood. Here she would have to begin by admitting how much remained unfamiliar.

Ember brought his nose close to the egg and held still. She watched the distance he left between his scales and its surface. Then she sat beside him and listened rather than trying to make the sound happen again.
The thought was so simple that it changed the chamber around her. What she had taken for a place of ancient secrets became a room full of lives that had not yet begun outside their shells.
Ember made a low note in his throat.
It travelled through the basin and into the walls. Water trembled in a hollow near Elara's foot. Farther away, another shell brightened.
The sound that answered did not come from an egg.
It was deeper. Beyond the chamber, beyond the falling water, somewhere in the mountain itself.
Elara stood and went towards the passage mouth. She looked back at Ember and the nests until a curve in the wall hid them from her.
Outside, the sun had almost reached the western ridge. Mist rose from the fall. Across the ravine, something vast moved in the shadow of the opposite cliff.
For an instant she thought the rock had shifted.
Then a wing opened.
It caught the last light along its upper edge before folding again. A horned head emerged from the dark, distant enough that she could not make out the colour of its eyes.
Elara did not move.
The creature looked towards the entrance. It did not cross the ravine or reach for her. After a while it lowered its head, and a second call rose from farther down the mountain.
She turned back to her son.
He stood inside the passage with one foot held carefully above the ground. He had followed because she had gone out of sight behind the curve of the wall.
Of course he had.
She walked to him and laid her hand against his face. Beyond the fall, the first great shape settled onto a ledge. She could not tell whether it had come to guard the entrance or only to listen.
She would not make a promise out of something she did not understand.
But there were others. He was not the only one left for the world to fear or love.
“You should see them,” she told him. “When you can walk without limping.”
He looked past her, nostrils wide. This time she let him listen as long as he wanted.
They stayed beside the heart-stone that night.
Elara made no attempt to leave before dark. The passage gave shelter, and a runnel of clean water followed one wall of the chamber. She found a dry place above it and spread out the cloak.

There was work to do. She rinsed the cloth around Ember's leg and replaced the part that had rubbed loose during the climb. She cleaned the dirt from her own hands. She counted the remaining food, then stopped counting and opened the bundle.

She found Nessa's knife beneath the folded map. She cleaned it, dried it and wrapped the blade again before setting it where she would find it in the morning. She would have to send it back one day, or bring it herself if there came a way to do that safely. The thought did not carry forgiveness with it. Nessa had helped them, and Nessa had failed them; Elara could remember both without making either untrue.

The cloak needed a stitch near its fastening. She had no needle. She tied the torn part for now, making an ugly knot she could undo later. There were things she could mend in the morning and things for which she did not yet have what was needed. It helped to keep them separate.
When she offered meat, he took it at once.
She laughed, properly this time, and had to pull the wrapping cloth back before he swallowed it with the next piece.
“That part isn't supper.”
His eyes followed the bundle. Hunger had returned before dignity, exactly as it always had.

She fed him what she could spare and ate the bread. It would not last long. Tomorrow she would need to find more. Beyond the mountain lay people who might see only a monster, and behind them lay a village whose losses would not disappear because they had survived.
None of those things had been solved by the light in the stone.

She thought of the girl beneath the cart and the man who had asked what to tell the village. She wanted a home in which she did not have to hide her son. She also wanted to be able to remember the people who had hurt her without seeing every person below the mountain as one of them. Neither wish was something the heart-stone could give her.
Ember nudged the empty wrapping. She turned it inside out to show him there was no more in that portion, and he sighed so extravagantly that she laughed.
“You've had the larger share.”

He examined the cloth in case she had missed anything. It was a familiar injustice, being finished with supper before he was finished being hungry. She let him investigate while she ate her last mouthful of bread. She needed food as well. She intended to be here to feed him tomorrow.
Yet she could think about tomorrow now. A place for water. A safer path. What he might be able to catch once his leg healed. Questions with answers she could look for while he was alive beside her.
Ember lowered his head onto the cloak.
She sat against his shoulder and watched the nearest egg. A fine line had appeared near its upper curve. Once, something tapped from the other side.
Her son opened one eye at the sound.
“We'll be here,” she said softly.
He closed it again.
For the first time since the cave where he was born, Elara let the dark gather without wondering how she would hide him when morning came.
She rested her hand beneath his jaw.

He did not stir to find out what she needed. His breath moved against her wrist, deep and even. Elara left her hand where it was and looked once towards the entrance, where the night beyond the falling water was blue rather than black.
He was warm.
